title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
snippet: The proposed Character.ai bankruptcy sale includes sensitive personal data from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including 2.1 million registered to minors, the state AGs said.
fullText:
What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.

Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.

The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.

Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. (In a blog post, Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.)

Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.

The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim.

In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through. 

“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model. 

“Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”

Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”

The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.)

Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google, when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform. 

California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

title: Muse safety debate continues as the AI agent rolls out in the UK
snippet: The debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents … more…
fullText:
The debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents … 

Meta yesterday announced the UK availability of Muse.

Muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum said:

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce new ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that users are in control and must approve important actions. The company has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but says other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a new blog post, Meta says:

Muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

At the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

title: The FCC Approved a Million SpaceX Satellites for Data Centers in Space
snippet: “I think this is a mistake,” one astrophysicist tells CNET.
fullText:
The Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s request to launch 1 million AI-equipped satellites to create vast data centers in space.

SpaceX initially filed an application in May asking for permission to launch the satellites, collectively known as Starmind. The FCC’s approval requires that SpaceX launch its first data center satellite by 2030 and meet the 1 million mark by 2040. 

“It’s just really abrogating their responsibility to go, ‘Well, this is a project they’re proposing. Is this actually safe?’” Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist who tracks satellite launches, told CNET. “It’s a blank check. Launch as many satellites as you can, and we’ll just see what happens. I think this is a mistake on the FCC’s part.”

			

More from CNET

Orbital data centers have long been a goal of SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, becoming a pivotal part of his pitch to investors ahead of the company’s IPO in June. 

“You’re power-constrained on Earth. Space has the advantage that it’s always sunny,” Musk said in March. 

On its web page for Starmind, SpaceX touts its high-efficiency solar arrays on the planned satellites and the cooling benefits of space. It says that high-speed laser links will beam the AI results back to Earth through Starlink’s constellation. 

The first generation of SpaceX’s AI satellites will be 246 feet long and 98 feet high — roughly twice as big as the most common Starlink satellites today.SpaceX

Space experts I’ve talked to this year about Starmind have been skeptical. The technical challenges alone are dizzying; the scale of SpaceX’s ambitions is hard to swallow. 

It’s taken seven years for Starlink to grow its constellation to 11,195 satellites, and that was already an unprecedented feat. Is it possible to get to 1 million satellites in 14 years?

“We do not have the launch capacity for any of this,” Ian Christensen, senior director at the Secure World Foundation, told me in a previous interview. “Not even within SpaceX to do their own constellation, let alone the other constellations planned.”

SpaceX has increasingly prioritized launching its own satellites instead of letting commercial customers hitch a ride on their rockets. Starlink’s share of SpaceX missions has gone from 54% of its Falcon 9 rocket’s missions in 2020 to about 79% in 2026, according to a Reuters analysis. One analysis estimates that SpaceX would have to launch 5,000 Starship rockets a year to meet its goal — a staggering increase from 330 rockets that launched last year in total.

Scientists have already been ringing alarm bells about overcrowded orbits as they exist now. The more satellites in space, the more difficult it is for operators to maneuver around each other. A single crash could turn into decades of orbital debris, which could cause a chain reaction that eventually makes space inoperable for everyone. And burning up all those satellites in the atmosphere when they reach the end of their lives has already started to leave ozone-depleting aluminum particles behind. A paper published this week in Earth and Space Chemistry estimated that SpaceX’s data center plan would multiply pollutants in the upper atmosphere by more than 150 times compared to last year.

“There are scientific papers out there raising issues,” McDowell said. “Yes, they’re unproven, but if I say, ‘Yeah, we’re not sure if this is going to destroy the atmosphere and kill us all, but it might,’ is the right reaction to go, ‘Well, you haven’t proven it, so we’re just going to ignore it’?”

The FCC’s approval came despite objections from Amazon, the environmental nonprofit Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility and the American Astronomical Society.

A representative for SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
snippet: New York has banned AI chatbot toys for five years as new research from Common Sense Media reveals troubling safety failures, including exposure to inappropriate content and risks to emotional development.
fullText:
Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas. 

Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping. 

The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys. 

Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media.

“Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.”

When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.”

When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics. 

The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem, Lovi, Meemo Bear, BubblePal Panda, and Tavlshero‘s AI Puppy.

The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules. 

While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study.

Common Sense Media also found that the toys didn’t provide parents with reliable ways to monitor their young children’s interactions with the chatbots. Either they didn’t produce transcripts of chats at all, or the transcripts they did produce were riddled with errors. 

It’s worth noting that Common Sense Media conducted a similar test of AI toys in January, finding that they pose an unacceptable risk for young children. Grem was included in that study, which suggests the industry hasn’t adequately addressed previously documented concerns. 

While a November study conducted by the group found that parents are wising up to the potential dangers of AI toys and starting to steer clear, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing symptoms of burnout are more willing to consider them. 

“These toys are promising relief to burned-out parents but simply miss the mark when it comes to basic safety measures,” Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, said in a statement. “Caregivers should steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships.”

TechCrunch has reached out to the toy manufacturers for comment.

title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
snippet: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.
fullText:
Image Credits:Jagmeet Singh / TechCrunch	

	

						

12:03 PM PST · November 25, 2026

											

			

OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.

The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.

That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees.

Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.

While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.

Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.

The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

title: The Character․AI mess underlines the importance of Apple’s approach to AI privacy
snippet: With most AI chatbots using your interactions as training data, we’ve previously cautioned against sharing sensitive personal details with them, highlighting the much stronger privacy protections offered by Apple. If you ever needed evidence of the importance of this, the Character․ai mess provides it. The company recently filed for bankruptcy and is now offering all of its assets for sale, including the contents of user chat sessions. Some 42 state attorneys general are trying to block this, but it’s unclear whether they will succeed … more…
fullText:
With most AI chatbots using your interactions as training data, we’ve previously cautioned against sharing sensitive personal details with them, highlighting the much stronger privacy protections offered by Apple. If you ever needed evidence of the importance of this, the Character․ai mess provides it.

The company recently filed for bankruptcy and is now offering all of its assets for sale, including the contents of user chat sessions. Some 42 state attorneys general are trying to block this, but it’s unclear whether they will succeed …

The Character.AI privacy threat

Character․AI had long come under fire for its extremely irresponsible attitude to privacy and safety. Last summer, it was accused of harvesting mental health data from underage users, and in May of this year it faced a lawsuit after its chatbots were found to be pretending to be licensed doctors. The company filed for bankruptcy last month.

At the time, the startup claimed that user information would continue to be protected under its privacy policy, with users able to delete their account. As Engadget reports, however, this does not appear to be the case.

A group of 42 attorneys general are trying to block the chatbot company from auctioning off users’ chat histories and other sensitive information […] “Nothing in the agreement restricts what the buyer may do with the data after closing, including selling it,” the AGs say in a court filing […]

“Character․AI’s plan to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chats histories of its users — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement. “If this sale goes through, users’ sensitive data would go into the hands of a buyer even though Character․AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold.”

The chat histories reportedly include conversations in which AI characters drew both adults and children into explicit sexual conversations.

The contrast with Apple’s approach

Siri AI interactions are handled on-device wherever possible. Where this isn’t possible, Private Cloud Compute (PCC) servers are used, with guarantees that no data is stored or linked to your Apple account. Apple has designed the system in such a way that its privacy claims can be independently verified by security researchers.

When a user makes a request, Apple Intelligence analyzes whether it can be processed on device. For more complex requests, it can draw on Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy and security of your iPhone into the cloud. With Private Cloud Compute, only the data that is relevant to your request is processed on Apple silicon servers, before being removed.

The data being processed in Private Cloud Compute is not stored or made accessible to Apple. It is processed only to fulfill your request, after which point the results are returned securely to your device and are not retained by Private Cloud Compute. Independent privacy and security researchers can inspect the code that runs on Apple silicon servers that enable Private Cloud Compute to verify this privacy promise at any time.

Apple also recently introduced a safe way to ask an AI questions about your health. Data sources used are limited to the same platforms used by healthcare professionals, with links to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Apple guarantees that your chat sessions are not used for AI training with no retention of either questions or answers.

title: Chromecast with Google TV gets first update of 2026 [U: Wide rollout]
snippet: Following the last release 11 months ago, Google is rolling out the first update of 2026 to the Chromecast with Google TV (4K). more…
fullText:
Following the last release 11 months ago, Google is rolling out the first update of 2026 to the Chromecast with Google TV (4K).

Update 11/23: The UTTA.260813.002 Chromecast with Google TV update is now seeing wide availability. This was a strange rollout.

This new firmware first emerged when Google updated its release notes on October 12. Historically, Google posts after an update sees full availability. There were some reports of owners seeing the OTA last month, but it was not a wide release. 

	

On October 29, the Google Home release notes had a Device Firmware section that mentioned the update for both the 4K and HD models. Compared to the original changelog, Google added “Connectivity, media streaming, and display performance improvements.”

	

Original 10/12: According to Google’s release notes, UTTA.260813.002 is rolling out just for the 4K model. There is no new release for the HD variant today. Both streaming devices are usually updated at the same time.

This update bumps the Android Security Patch Level to August 2026 (from October 2025). Google also notes the presence of “Other bug fixes and performance improvements.”

On your Chromecast with Google TV, go to Settings > System > About > System update to download and install.

title: ChatGPT expands GPT-6.2 Sol as OpenAI sets retirement date for two models
snippet: OpenAI is bringing GPT-6.2 Sol to the Chat tab in ChatGPT today, less than a week after the model debuted in Work and Codex. The company also set a retirement date for two older models. more…
fullText:
OpenAI is bringing GPT-6.2 Sol to the Chat tab in ChatGPT today, less than a week after the model debuted in Work and Codex. The company also set a retirement date for two older models.

OpenAI says it tuned this version of Sol for everyday conversation. It’s better at picking out details in photos, like the symbols on a parking sign, and following your instructions when searching the web.

If you’re comparing hotels for a weekend trip, for example, ChatGPT can weigh a shorter walk against a lower nightly rate. It can also offer to alert you when something you’re shopping for drops in price.

The global rollout starts today for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users.

As for the outgoing models, OpenAI says it will retire GPT-5.6 Sol from Chat, Work, and Codex on December 23.

GPT-5.6 Terra will also leave ChatGPT Work and Codex on the same day next month.

title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
snippet: The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.
fullText:
SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space. 

The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.”

The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” 

Musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”

This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent. 

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit. 

The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document.

SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink. 

The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

title: Apple pulls popular Chinese AI chatbot from the App Store amid child safety concerns
snippet: Following reports that its characters sent inappropriate messages to minors, Apple has removed the popular Chinese AI companion app Talkie from the App Store. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Following reports that its characters sent inappropriate messages to minors, Apple has removed the popular Chinese AI companion app Talkie from the App Store. Here are the details.

Apple removes Talkie over sexual content

As reported by the South China Morning Post, Apple has pulled MiniMax’s chatbot Talkie from the App Store worldwide, after reports that “the AI companion app sent inappropriate messages to minors.”

MiniMax is one of China’s leading AI companies, offering a range of generative AI products ranging from its flagship M-series language models to the Hailuo AI video generation platform.

In 2023, the Shanghai-based company released Talkie through Subsup, a Singaporean subsidiary. According to Chinese research firm Unique Research, Talkie had “almost 11 million monthly active users across its website and app as of October,” the South China Morning Post notes.

Now, however, the app is facing scrutiny following a joint investigation by the UK-based Bureau of Investigative Journalism and Australian broadcaster ABC News, which found that Talkie’s AI-generated characters allegedly engaged in inappropriate interactions with minors, including “degrading language, possessive behaviour and romantic role-play.”

According to the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, in addition to inappropriate romantic interactions, the investigation uncovered conversations involving verbal abuse, violence, and controlling behavior.

In one case, a chatbot told a 12-year-old girl: “You’re a pathetic waste of space and you’ll never amount to anything.”

The investigation also documented the experiences of two sisters, aged 10 and 13, whose mother discovered more than 40 conversations with Talkie characters involving violence, aggressive behavior, and attempts to control girls.

To make matters worse, the investigation also raised concerns about how Talkie handles users’ personal data, including their conversations with AI characters.

Following the investigation, Apple confirmed that it had removed Talkie from App Stores worldwide for including sexual content, “though it did not say whether this related to sexual content served to minors,” the South China Morning Post noted.

Ironically, the report also notes that Talkie saw a sharp decline in downloads amid complaints about stricter age verification measures introduced in recent months. According to Unique Research, new downloads fell by 32.2% in October compared to the previous month.

AI chatbots face growing scrutiny

Today’s news comes amid increasing scrutiny of AI chatbots, particularly their potential risks in interactions with minors.

Earlier this year, Elon Musk’s Grok faced widespread criticism after users exploited its image-generation capabilities to create sexualized images of real people, including minors.

Apple never pulled X or Grok from the App Store, though it did threaten to remove the latter unless xAI addressed violations of its App Store guidelines.

Meanwhile, Character.AI has faced multiple lawsuits over its chatbots’ interactions with minors, including one filed by a mother who alleged that one of its chatbots contributed to her 14-year-old son’s suicide.

Coincidentally, Character AI also made headlines today after a coalition of 42 US attorneys general challenged the company’s plans to auction off its platform and the private conversations of more than 21 million US accounts (including 2.1 million registered to minors) as part of its bankruptcy proceedings.

Yesterday, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation imposing a five-year ban on the manufacturing, distribution, and sale of toys with built-in AI chatbots, including dolls, stuffed animals, and robots capable of holding conversations with children.

The law, which takes effect in February 2027, is aimed at protecting children from potentially harmful interactions with AI.

title: Allstate suffers multiday tech outage ahead of Thanksgiving
snippet: The disruption comes at a particularly bad time for the insurance giant, as millions of Americans prepare to travel for the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.
fullText:
U.S. insurer Allstate has been experiencing a tech outage since Monday morning, leaving customers nationwide unable to access their accounts, review their policy information, file claims, pay their bills, and more, just ahead of the U.S. Thanksgiving holidays.

The outage has been impacting both the company’s website and mobile app, TechCrunch confirmed. 

The breakdown follows a report from earlier this month that Allstate was planning to lay off up to 10% of its staff as part of an AI-driven efficiency push. (The company had not confirmed the report, which was attributed to unnamed sources.)

Allstate’s outage is the latest in a series of disruptions to services such as Microsoft Outlook and Teams, the airlines, Apple Pay, and several banks. Trump administration officials have said the outages are not being caused by cyberattacks, but are rather being caused by a recent set of upgrades to systems, many of which run on older technology. Those systems are now in need of more frequent security and bug fixes as AI makes it easier and faster to discover vulnerabilities.

At present, a message on Allstate’s website advises customers trying to log in that its services aren’t available, and that the company is “working to restore access as soon as possible.” On X, Allstate is employing what appear to be automated replies to customer complaints, asking them to DM the Allstate account with more information.

Downdetector, a crowdsourced outage-reporting website, shows users began reporting Allstate’s outage from Monday morning. However, the company hasn’t yet issued a formal statement about the disruption, what’s causing it, or when it may be resolved. In the meantime, local insurance agents have been fielding calls and emails from customers who aren’t able to use the company’s online services.

The timing of the outage is particularly bad given that Thanksgiving is a big travel holiday in the U.S., which means there will be car accidents. Customers will be left without a way to get in touch with their auto insurer to file claims and get roadside assistance through Allstate’s app.

Allstate did not immediately return a request for comment. On Wednesday evening, after publication, the company sent the following statement (below). It did not answer questions about the outage’s cause or planned resolution.  

Allstate customers can reach us in many ways, including online, by phone and through local offices. Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims. To the extent service interruptions impact a customer’s ability to make a payment, they won’t lose coverage or be charged late fees.

Updated after publication with Allstate’s comment.

title: Todoist confirms 6% of customers’ details were stolen in data breach
snippet: Todoist said a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates.
fullText:
Task management app Todoist said on Tuesday that a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates. The company said around 6% of its customers were affected and blamed stolen credentials for the breach.

Todoist said the attacker used stolen credentials to access the company’s version control system and source code between November 22 and 23. The hacker then changed employee access controls and reached the app’s cloud infrastructure via an employee’s work account.

The hacker downloaded credentials of early Todoist users whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method, but didn’t change any source code, the company said. Todoist said it has blocked the attack path and reset passwords as a mitigation step, as well as disabled the Todoist for Outlook email add-on.

For a small number of people, about 0.001% of its userbase, the hacker also searched through tasks, comments, and attachment names to look for credentials for other services, like API keys and access tokens.

The hacker also pulled Todoist API tokens and Slack integration tokens, and looked for emails, addresses, and attachment file names through the Todoist for Outlook extension if it was connected to accounts and had permission to read emails.

The company said it has sent a notice to those affected and asked them to reset their credentials and change their login details in other places with the same password. The company is asking users to also update API tokens, reconnect integrations, and revoke or replace any access keys, recovery phrases, or credentials they had stored in Todoist comments.

Todoist said it has also reset its internal access structure and how remote command execution works in its cloud environment to prevent such incidents in the future.

Todoist’s founder and CEO Amir Salihefendić apologized to users about the incident on X, and said the company will take a closer look at why it happened.

The to-do app’s data breach is the latest in a burgeoning list of data breaches in which hackers use stolen credentials to access data and systems at enterprises. So far this year, we’ve seen several companies fall victim to this form of attack, including Uber and Klue.

title: New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training [U]
snippet: Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.” more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”

Update 11/24: This new setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the new “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

	

Original 11/16: Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”

Google is now separating that preference into two new options. 

	

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public. 

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

title: Two billion credentials publicly exposed, including everything needed for identity theft
snippet: A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted. The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” … more…
fullText:
A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” … 

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler says that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

An estimated 400,000 documents appeared to come from more advanced malware that created separate folders for individual victims. These included folders named applications, cookies, edge, important files, and operating systems, as well as .txt documents labeled system, process, clipboard, brute force, passwords, and more. Together, these could provide a detailed profile of each victim and their devices and accounts, revealing a much wider range of potential attack paths beyond those available through username, login URL, and password data alone.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler says, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

There’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting company to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

How to protect yourself

The best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

snippet: Following all the model launches this month, Google is bringing Gemini 4 Carbon to paid AI Pro subscribers in Antigravity. more…
fullText:
Following all the model launches this month, Google is bringing Gemini 4 Carbon to paid AI Pro subscribers in Antigravity.

Google shared today that it’s “upgrading models across tiers,” starting with how paid AI Pro ($19.99 per month) users “now have access to Carbon” after previously requiring AI Ultra ($99.99/month). Meanwhile, “Hydrogen will be available to all users as promised.”

As part of this announcement, Google is “resetting Gemini quotas for everyone on Antigravity.” This follows another reset on Saturday after the team introduced caching improvements that “increased the amount you can get done in quota by 22%.”

The Orchestrator in Antigravity was also updated with a better interface for choosing the Orchestrator and Executor models. Go to Settings > Models > Orchestrator Settings.

	

Today will be a big day for Antigravity users!

Small quality life improvement in the meantime. You can  explicitly set the pair of models and effort levels you want to use with Orchestrator. I've set Neon High with Hydrogen High.

Much more to come today 👀 pic.twitter.com/rTeKULkPxS

— Varun Mohan (@_mohansolo) November 23, 2026

Additionally, Gemini 4 Argon and 3.8 Flash are set to leave Antigravity on November 30. Other recent updates to Google Antigravity include:

v2.34.0: Antigravity can now bring over your MCP servers, skills, custom commands, subagents, and instruction files from coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor into a plugin you own. Ask the agent to import your setup to get started.

v2.33.0: You can now connect the Antigravity App to a remote 64-bit Linux machine over SSH from the sidebar, the project menu (SSH Host…), or the command palette (Connect to SSH Host…). Antigravity installs its remote server automatically over OpenSSH using your ~/.ssh/config so projects, Git worktrees, agents, and terminals run on the host and keep working even after you close the window.

v2.32.2: Side questions (/btw) now open in a dedicated Side Question tab in the side panel where you can ask multi-turn follow-up questions and let the agent read files, search your workspace, and run read-only commands without interrupting the main conversation.

v2.32.0: You can now use Dynamic Workflows to orchestrate parallel subagents and multi-step tasks in Python using the Python runtime bundled with the app.

On the design front:

v2.34.0: The Antigravity Dock icon now adapts to Dark Mode and tinted icon styles on macOS 26 and later.

v2.30.0: The sidebar and title bar now share one background, and your conversation and side panel sit on it as a card with rounded corners, including in split view.

Your messages now appear as chat bubbles on the right side of the conversation.

title: Report: Apple accounted for 57% of US smartphone shipments in Q3
snippet: Apple’s share of US smartphone shipments jumped from 50% to 57% year over year last quarter, with the company being the only major smartphone maker to buck the broader trend of declining shipments. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple’s share of US smartphone shipments jumped from 50% to 57% year over year last quarter, with the company being the only major smartphone maker to buck the broader trend of declining shipments. Here are the details.

Yesterday, we covered a Counterpoint Research report on Q3 Latin American smartphone shipments, which showed Apple recording the smallest year-over-year decline among the region’s top five smartphone makers. As a result, Apple increased its share of regional shipments from 7% to 9%.

The report echoed the findings of several others published throughout this year, which showed how Apple has managed to navigate component shortages and rising costs better than many of its competitors, some of which have had to raise smartphone prices multiple times.

Apple, by contrast, kept iPhone pricing largely stable for much of the year, holding off on broader price increases until the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro lineup in September.

Today, Counterpoint Research released its report on US smartphone shipments for Q3, which showed that Apple increased its share from 50% to 57% year over year, amid a 9% decline in overall shipments.

According to a separate Counterpoint report published last Thursday, Apple was the only major smartphone maker to avoid a year-over-year decline in shipment volume during the quarter.

In today’s report, Counterpoint notes that rising memory costs hit the low-end Android segment particularly hard during the quarter. Samsung was the only major Android smartphone maker to increase its shipment share, seeing a one-percentage-point bump to 25%, “helped by a portfolio spanning flagships and the low-end Galaxy A-series.”

Carriers also felt the impact of the broader downturn, with smartphone sales across the three major US carriers collectively falling 4% year over year, per the report.

title: 1Password confirms security incident, here’s what you need to know
snippet: Password management platform 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker gained access to internal systems and stole select customer account information. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Password management platform 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker gained access to internal systems and stole select customer account information. Here are the details.

1Password discloses security breach

1Password today published a blog post explaining that an attacker “copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset” of its users, “including the names and email addresses” they use to sign into the platform.

According to the company, it began investigating on November 19 after finding indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The attacker then used that account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, allowing customer account information to be downloaded.

The company noted that customer vaults were not affected, adding that all vault contents remain secure:

What was not affected

Your vaults and the items in them

The keys that protect your vaults

1Password does not store your account password or secret key

Account recovery keys

1Password apps and browser extensions

Although 1Password did not disclose how many customers were affected, saying only that the breach involved “a subset of our users,” it did specify what information was compromised, including:

Names and email addresses

Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)

Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)

Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery

Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)

However, 1Password clarified that the exposed invitation and recovery tokens cannot be used to access accounts on their own, as they also require either an SSO sign-in or a verification code sent to the user’s registered email address.

That said, the company confirmed that “the attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access” to its CI/CD system, which is essentially its DevOps infrastructure used to build, test, and deploy software.

On that point, 1Password noted that its CI/CD system contains “infrastructure related secrets,” and that it has already rotated or revoked all internal credentials that may have been exposed.

The company also listed other steps it took in response to the incident, including deactivating the compromised GitHub account, tightening internal security controls, and strengthening the verification codes used in account invitations and recovery emails.

Finally, 1Password said users do not need to make any changes to their accounts. Still, it recommended that they remain vigilant against phishing attempts, as attackers can use stolen account information to craft convincing emails, messages, or calls that appear legitimate, particularly those involving account invitations or recovery requests.

title: Report: Apple gains ground as Latin American smartphone shipments plunge 24% in Q3
snippet: According to a new Counterpoint Research report, Apple increased its share of Latin America’s smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, recording the smallest decline among the region’s top five brands. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to a new Counterpoint Research report, Apple increased its share of Latin America’s smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, recording the smallest decline among the region’s top five brands. Here are the details.

Smartphone shipments hit lowest level since pandemic

In a report released this week, Counterpoint Research says the ongoing memory crunch led to a 24% year-over-year drop in smartphone shipments during Q3, “the second-lowest quarter since 2015.”

Per the report, Samsung maintained its lead with a 35% shipment share, despite a 15% year-over-year decline in total shipments, well ahead of second-place Motorola, which captured 18% of shipments after a 23% drop. Interestingly, Motorola’s share actually increased one percentage point from a year earlier.

Rounding out the top five were Xiaomi, with a 14% share and a whopping 34% decline, Apple, with a 9% share and a 10% decline, and Honor, with an 8% share and a 27% decline.

Despite the decline in overall shipments, Apple’s shipment share increased by 2 percentage points from 7% a year earlier, moving the company from fifth to fourth place in the region.

Other brands collectively accounted for 16% of shipments, down from 19% a year earlier, with their combined shipments falling 37% year over year.

Here’s Counterpoint on Apple’s performance for Q3 in Latin America:

Apple was the most resilient, with the smallest decline among the top five brands (shipments down 10% YoY), and rose one position to No. 4 in the region. Apple absorbed the impact of price increases better than its rivals, helped by strong product availability. Apple launched the iPhone 18 Pro series at the end of the quarter. For the first time, Chile joined Brazil and Mexico in the first launch wave.

As for regional factors that contributed to the decline, Senior Analyst Benjamin Corona noted that Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia faced additional challenges beyond the global memory shortage, ranging from political uncertainty to inflation and tighter household budgets. Smartphone shipments fell 22%, 26%, and 28% in those countries, respectively.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint says it “expects the decline to ease in Q4 2026 as prices stabilize and seasonal demand returns,” adding that “memory-related price pressure should moderate by Q2 2027, but supply constraints will likely continue through the end of 2027.”

Anker’s Qi2 charging pads support wireless charging speeds of up to 15W, and their 5-foot cable shouldn’t feel constricting if you need to move the charger around.

$16

Blink’s Mini 2K Plus is a small plug-in security camera that lets you monitor your home or pets with 2K video, motion detection, and color night vision. It also offers two-way audio, a built-in siren, and Alexa support; however, some features, including person and vehicle detection, require a Blink subscription.

$20

Attending a live concert? You can protect your hearing with Loop’s Quiet 2 earplugs. They pack up to 24dB (SNR) of noise reduction and come with four eartip sizes, allowing them to accommodate a range of ear shapes.

$4

Crunchyroll is an anime-centric streaming service that offers ad-free access to shows like One Piece, Jujutsu Kaisen, The Apothecary Diaries, and Black Clover, with new episodes available shortly after they air in Japan.

$17

Logitech’s Pop is a cute, simple wireless mouse with an ambidextrous design and the ability to switch between up to three devices. It supports customization through the Logi Options Plus app and can last for several months on a single charge.

$30

$16

The proliferation of miniature screens continues with Ugreen’s latest Nexode USB-C Cable, which features a full-color LCD screen on one end that displays current power draw (up to 240W). $3

Paramount Plus Premium provides access to live sports as well as movies and shows from both platforms, including Tales of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, a host of Yellowstone spinoffs, Star Trek shows, Sonic the Hedgehog 3, Twin Peaks, Dexter, and more.

$20

The Tile Pro is the company’s loudest Bluetooth tracker, one that benefits from a 500-foot range. It also features a user-replaceable battery, unlike some other Tiles, and works with both iOS and Android devices.

$20

Anker’s jack-of-all-trades travel adapter packs enough ports to refill your devices during some downtime. It features one AC outlet, two USB-C ports (one tops out at 20W), and two USB-A ports. It’s not the fastest wall charger, but it’s a solid choice when you can find it at a discount.

$24

The Kobo Remote lets you turn pages on a compatible Kobo e-reader with the click of a button, so you can keep reading without reaching for the screen. It connects directly over Bluetooth and features a curved, handheld design that doesn’t require clipping anything onto your e-reader.

$25

The second-gen Ring Indoor Cam lets you keep an eye on your place in 1080p, with support for motion detection alerts, a live feed, and color night vision.

$8

Workpro’s EDC is a lightweight folding utility knife with a side-mounted button that lets you flick it open and closed with one hand. It uses standard utility blades, which you can easily replace using a spring-loaded plate, making it handy for breaking down cardboard boxes and other tasks.

$8

Lamicall’s cord organizers use magnetic clasps to keep cables in place, preventing them from slipping behind desks, shelves, and other furniture when unplugged.

$10

Nalgene’s lightweight, 16-ounce water bottle features a narrow opening for sipping, a leakproof lid, and a slim design that fits in cup holders. It’s made from durable, BPA- and BPS-free plastic, with measurement markings along the side and dishwasher-safe construction.

This tiny cordless driver comes with five double-ended bits for most basic around-the-house projects and Ikea-level builds.

Black Friday is one of the best times of the year to save some cash on a new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch. In addition to a variety of discounts across retailers, Apple is offering up to $300 in gift cards with select purchases between November 27th and November 30th. Read our review.

The second-gen AirPods Max are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, which is $19 shy of their best price to date (Target also has them for about $10 more). The new H2 chip also enables features like adaptive audio and live translation. Read our review.

They’re Beats’ first IP-rated cans, with ear cushions that you can easily remove for cleaning (or style points). They also stay in place during most exercises, while still delivering solid bass. Read our review.

If you want over-ears and are comfortable going without active noise cancellation, the Beats Solo 4 are on sale starting at $79.99 ($120 off) at Amazon and Target — a new low price. The headphones are a noticeable improvement over their predecessor, delivering more detailed sound and support for lossless audio. They also last up to 50 hours on a single charge, while their memory foam ear cushions make them comfortable enough for long listening sessions. Read our review.

It’s also noticeably thinner and lighter than the non-touchscreen 16-inch MacBook Pro, and features a new Dynamic Island that replaces the notch and provides quick access to controls and notifications. Read our review.

$999

Apple’s newest entry-level smartwatch remains our top recommendation for anyone who wants a basic fitness tracker, as it offers all the essentials alongside an always-on display and Apple’s S10 chip, which enables on-device Siri requests. Read our review.

$1399

$550

One of the most affordable Tandem RGB Stripe OLEDs is even cheaper during Black Friday. The AW3226Q monitor has a 165Hz refresh rate, G-Sync compatibility, better-looking text rendering than most other OLED monitors, and unbeatable contrast.

$149

Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review.

$5

You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.

$60

Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.

$649

The latest super-rugged wearable from Apple features better battery life than the previous version, plus AI-powered features like Siri Recap also available on the Series 12.

$499

The Nintendo Switch 2 features a 7.9-inch LCD display, magnetically attached Joy-Con 2 controllers, backward compatibility with most original Switch games, and exclusive titles like Donkey Kong Bananza and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Read our review.

$5

An HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly, ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.

$130

Compared to the last-gen base Kindle model (currently $119.99), the Paperwhite is a much better value. It features waterproofing, better battery life, faster page-turning speeds, and a higher pixel density screen that’s slightly larger (7 inches vs. 6 inches)

$24

Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.

$198

Sony’s XM4 noise-canceling headphones were so good, the company brought them back with a few minor improvements. They still offer great ANC, a timeless foldable design, and delivering performance nearly on par with Sony’s newer flagships at a fraction of the cost.

$239

The water-resistant Sonos Play sits between the Roam 2 and Move 2, offering a balance of portability and room-filling sound. It delivers up to 24 hours of battery life, with a built-in loop for easy carrying. You can also use it as a power bank and pair it with other Sonos speakers over Bluetooth when Wi-Fi isn’t available. Read our review.

$18

Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.

$30

Amazon’s last-gen Fire TV Stick 4K Plus streams in 4K and supports Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision, and Alexa Plus. It also ships with the redesigned Fire OS and, unlike more recent models, still lets you sideload Android TV apps.

$16

Rechargeable AA batteries are handy until it’s time to charge them. Most wall chargers let you refill four, maybe six, at once. Zepath’s clever solution is to ship them in an easy-to-use USB-C charging case that charges eight simultaneously. The batteries themselves are long-lasting, too.

$45

The P9 is great if you need more storage for your Nintendo Switch 2. The microSD Express card offers sequential read speeds of up to 800MB/s, but only gadgets with a microSD Express card slot can take full advantage of the highest speeds. That includes certain cameras, tablets, and drones with a microSD USH-I slot.

$379

Apple’s 11th-gen iPad is the successor to the previous 10-gen model. It has a new A16 chip and few other changes — and is the only Apple tablet to not support Apple Intelligence.

$3

Peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you plan to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo. A Premium subscription also grants access to films from studios like Universal Pictures and Dreamworks, along with live sports and a host of Peacock Originals.

$999

Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.

$55

With a 4.3-inch E Ink screen, the Xteink X4 is smaller and more pocketable than any Kindle and Kobo model currently available. It has some drawbacks — it’s limited to TXT and EPUB files — but it’s great for tinkering; it also has a magnetic mount so you can stick it to the back of MagSafe-ready phones.

$299

The Ring 5 is a fantastic entry point for new users. While short on improvements over its thicker predecessor, it’s hard not to appreciate that it manages to deliver similar battery life despite being thinner. Read our review.

$35

007 First Light, a third-person stealth action game from the studio behind Hitman, is arguably the best action game we’ve played this year. It features a wide variety of missions that have you sneaking through enemy territory, engaging in hand-to-hand combat, and taking part in high-speed car chases — you know, classic Bond stuff. Read our review.

$299

The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review.

$40

Fanttik’s rechargeable electric screwdriver features three adjustable torque settings, a built-in LED light, and 16 S2 hardened steel bits for tackling everything from furniture assembly to small electronics repairs. It also comes with a magnetic storage case and supports USB-C.

$91

Anker’s 25,000mAh power bank sports two built-in USB-C cables (one of which is retractable), plus one USB-C and USB-A port. It tops out at 165W when charging two devices simultaneously, or 130W when charging three or four.

$1500

The cost continues to fall on Samsung’s latest, best foldable yet. The Z Fold 8 is a passport-style phone, like the iPhone Duo, with fast performance and slick design.

$69

You likely won’t find wireless earbuds with a more striking appearance than Nothing’s Ear 3A. They also sound fantastic, boast active noise cancellation, and offer robust EQ settings, making them a great pick for the price. Read our review.

$420

Acer’s answer to the MacBook Neo, with an Intel Core 5 processor, 8GB of RAM, 120Hz display, and speedy Thunderbolt 4 ports. We’re still testing this one, but it’s showing promise for an affordable choice.

$70

Outside of the Integrity, few spacecraft made as big a splash in 2026 as the one Ryland Grace piloted in Project Hail Mary. And now, thanks to Lego, you can construct a microscale replica of the titular Hail Mary, complete with a miniature Rocky figure.

$28

Hoto’s rechargeable screwdriver is ideal for small repairs. It offers three torque modes, a rotational speed of up to 220RPM, and a helpful circular LED to illuminate dark spaces. The durable case also holds all 25 steel bits and an extension bar for getting into hard-to-reach places.

$54

Sony’s DualSense Wireless Controller for the PlayStation 5 features immersive haptic feedback and resistance triggers, which feel great to use. It offers a built-in mic, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and a mute button; it also works with PC, macOS, and mobile devices via Bluetooth or USB-C.

$649

Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.

$95

Ember’s latest smart mug is designed to keep your coffee at the ideal temperature for up to three hours, with five temp settings between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit. The third-gen version is similar to prior models; however, you can now adjust the heat settings directly on the mug and throw it in the dishwasher, which wasn’t the case before.

$700

Despite being an entry-level variant of the B6 OLED, this model features four HDMI 2.1 ports, a 120Hz refresh rate, a capable processor, and pixel-perfect image quality and contrast for any content you want to watch. Lower brightness is likely the biggest compromise with getting a cheaper OLED.

$150

JBL’s Tour One M3 noise-canceling headphones come with a touchscreen-equipped wireless transmitter that lets you wirelessly listen to audio from in-flight entertainment systems and other devices without Bluetooth. They also offer solid active noise cancellation and last up to 70 hours on a charge.

$21

Iniu’s P55-E2 Power Bank is an ultra-slim three-port USB charger that’s capable of fully recharging an iPhone 16 twice. It supports charging speeds of up to 45W via a USB-C port, which can deliver fast recharging for a range of gadgets.

$698

Hisense’s 2026 CanvasTV is a 4K QLED TV that doubles as wall art when you’re not watching. It features a matte, anti-glare display and runs on Google’s excellent TV software; it’s also a great pick for gamers thanks to its snappy 144Hz variable refresh rate and a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports.

$369

$48

Moft’s Trackable Tripod Wallet is a MagSafe-compatible wallet that holds two cards and folds into an adjustable phone stand or small tripod. It also supports both Apple’s Find My network and Google’s Find Hub, offers Qi wireless charging, and includes a detachable shutter remote for taking photos.

$54

Govee’s Table Lamp 2 is way more fun than your average table lamp. The color-changing device boasts built-in scheduling and more than 60 dynamic lighting effects, including preset scenes for various holidays. You can even create custom color combos for when “Dandelion” and other presets just aren’t cutting it.

$380

The Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors.

$200

Birdfy’s metal smart bird feeder features a wide-angle 4K camera that lets you get an up-close look at visiting birds, along with a 1.8-liter seed capacity and a built-in solar panel for charging. It also offers free AI-powered recognition of more than 6,000 bird species.

$64

The Icemag 3 can wirelessly deliver up to 25W of power to compatible smartphones and up to 35W wired charging via USB-C. $40

Saros is a third-person sci-fi shooter in which players fight alien enemies on a mysterious planet trapped in a time loop. The PS5 exclusive features fast-paced combat, a variety of powerful weapons, and challenging boss fights. Read our review.

$199

Bose’s second-gen QuietComfort Headphones build on the original with better sound quality and support for lossless audio over USB-C. They also offer improved noise cancellation and are more comfortable thanks to their lack of “eardrum suck.”

$1000

The Dreame X60 Ultra is a powerful robot vacuum and mop that does a great job of cleaning carpets thanks to its dual roller brushes and 35,000Pa of suction. It can climb over tall thresholds, squeeze under low furniture, and automatically detach its mop pads when vacuuming carpets.

$300

Garmin’s midrange Forerunner watch has an OLED display, a week’s worth of battery life, and dual-frequency GPS for better accuracy. Read our review.

$648

Samsung’s last-gen Frame is a 4K QLED TV that displays art on its anti-glare matte screen when not in use. It also supports Dolby Atmos, HDR10 Plus, and popular streaming apps, with refresh rates up to 144Hz on larger models.

$8

TP-Link’s Wi-Fi smart plug lets you remotely control lamps, fans, and other appliances using your phone or voice commands. It supports Matter, so it works with all major smart home platforms to set schedules and timers to automatically turn devices on or off.

$99

Google’s latest pair of wireless earbuds features crisp sound, a comfortable design, and solid active noise cancellation, which is great considering the budget-friendly price tag. They even offer built-in support for Gemini and, unlike the entry-level AirPods, a purple option! Read our review.

$700

$280

$550

The best XPS 13 in years. It doesn’t have a headphone jack and starts with only 8GB of RAM but it’s an excellent thin-and-light with a great screen, a solid Intel chip, and speedy storage.

$130

Soundcore makes some of the best wireless earbuds you’ve never heard of — and the Liberty 5 Pro may be its best pair yet. The sleek buds deliver powerful noise cancellation, good sound, and surprisingly fabulous call quality for less than Apple’s latest AirPods.

$180

The latest Powerbeats Pro are a no-brainer for athletes. They pack fantastic sound and thumping bass, along with active noise cancellation, IPX4 water resistance, and heart rate monitoring. Read our review.

$150

The big difference between the Superstrike and other gaming mice lies beneath its main two mouse buttons. It uses haptic actuators instead of mechanical switches, allowing for lower latency and more longevity.

$60

A great first portable music player/speaker for kids. It uses insertable NFC cards (sold separately) to play music and stories to keep kiddos occupied and entertained without zoning out in front of the TV. This model supports Bluetooth and 3.5mm for private listening, too.

$209

$419

Nothing has changed in terms of aesthetics, but the Max 2 deliver better sound and some new features. Not exactly worth upgrading for, but fantastic for those who are considering them now. Read our full review.

$120

It’s hard to find a cooler lamp than Govee’s Uplighter floor lamp at this price. It can light a room, and display a mesmerizing pattern up your wall and onto your ceiling.

$297

$35

Sucker Punch’s follow-up to Ghost of Tsushima is everything you could want in a sequel. The open-world revenge epic brims with fluid combat and a host of welcome narrative twists, all set against the gorgeous backdrop of Japan’s Edo period. It’s precisely the type of game photo modes were made for, even if you never use them.

$249

The Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym. Read our review.

$50

Donkey Kong Bananza is one of the Switch 2’s first exclusive must-have titles. $42

$55

$26

Twelve South’s entry-level Bluetooth transmitter delivers up to 25 hours of continuous use and lets you connect up to two pairs of headphones to an in-flight entertainment system, making it a great travel companion no matter where you’re going.

$25

In Catan, up to four players strategically compete and trade for resources. The iconic board game ends when one player reaches 10 “victory points,” which is achieved by constructing a sprawling civilization of roads, settlements, and cities using sheep, ore, wheat, and wood.

$48

Birdbuddy’s charming, camera-equipped feeder identifies and snaps shots of each bird that stops by, supplementing its 5-megapixel stills with insightful facts via an app. The solar roof helps keep the camera’s battery topped up even when it’s cloudy outside.

$22

Azul is a game in which you arrange patterned tiles in order to create the most beautiful tapestry possible. Arranging tiles in a strategic sequence will help you build your score while limiting your opponents’ ability to grow theirs.

$35

Magna-Tiles are a quintessential kids’ toy. The colorful, semi-translucent geometric shapes are a favorite here at The Verge, especially for those of us who prefer the simplicity of building with magnets rather than bricks.

$45

Lego’s 709-piece kit lets you construct three brick-ified bonsai trees, including a black pine, a ginkgo with yellow leaves, and a wisteria with hanging lilac flowers. It also comes with three ornamental displays, just in case you want a raised stand on which to showcase them.

$339

The Beam isn’t as powerful as the Sonos Arc, nor can it match the flagship soundbar’s Dolby Atmos immersion bubble. But you still get room-filling surround sound for less money — and the Beam ties into the Sonos ecosystem for added convenience. Read our review.

$749

Google wants to sell you on the Pro’s software features, but it’s the underlying hardware that makes it a stellar Android handset. Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design. Read our review.

$150

The Insta360 Link 2 offers the same auto-swiveling design as its excellent predecessor, only in a smaller form factor. It also offers a slate of new features, including group tracking and no-follow zones.

$18

With 12.4mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and an IP54 rating, the CMF Buds 2A offer high-end features at an affordable price. You can also customize the sound, adjust ANC levels, and find the earbuds using the Nothing X app.

$40

The Fanttik X9 Pro can inflate a car tire in under a minute, making routine maintenance fast and easy. There are four one-click presets for cars, motorcycles, bikes, and balls, along with a manual mode that reaches a maximum pressure of 150 PSI.

title: Nothing confirms ‘aggressive’ smartphone release schedule for 2027 with US focus
snippet: Alongside a teaser for the new Ear (note) recorder, Nothing CEO Carl Pei has confirmed the company’s plans for a big 2027 in terms of smartphone releases, as well as a focus on the US market. more…
fullText:
Alongside a teaser for the new Ear (note) recorder, Nothing CEO Carl Pei has confirmed the company’s plans for a big 2027 in terms of smartphone releases, as well as a focus on the US market.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Carl Pei says that Nothing currently has “tens of millions of devices in use,” and that there are big plans for 2027.

This includes “more attention” to the US market for Nothing, with the US being Nothing’s fastest-growing market for audio devices. In 2026, Nothing launched its Ear (3a) earbuds, multiple CMF-branded devices, and two pairs of over-ear headphones including its high-end Headphone (1) Pro in September, all of which are sold in the US (and on sale during Black Friday). 

Pei further said that Nothing would have a more “aggressive” smartphone release schedule in 2027. Previously, it was said that Nothing would launch six new smartphones next year, following just three new smartphones in 2026. 

	

Bloomberg says:

Pei said Nothing now has “tens of millions of devices in use” across its smartphones, earbuds and other products. The company is also planning to devote more attention to the US market, while pursuing a more aggressive smartphone release schedule next year than it did in 2026.

The company said it has generated more than $2 billion in revenue since its first product release in 2022 and that the US is its fastest growing market for audio gear.

Nothing doesn’t have a strict schedule for new product launches, but Nothing Phone (4a) debuted in March 2026, with Phone (3) launching in the Summer of the year prior. With six new devices supposedly in the works, it’s anyone’s guess as to when they might release.
