title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
snippet: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model development.
fullText:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”

“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”

The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”

Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.” 

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power. 

Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.  

Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”

Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.

In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”

“As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control. 

Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations. 

In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently. 

“Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”

title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
snippet: Amazon and Meta are discussing a potential deal that would end a two-month-long blockade of Muse.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

6:10 AM PST · November 25, 2026

Image Credits:Meta

		

							

											
									

					

	

Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store.

The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.

According to a Wednesday report by Fortune, citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.

One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.

Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.

Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter.

Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported.

Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.

title: AI Mode adding Google Drive, Wallet, & Gemini app integration
snippet: Personal Intelligence in AI Mode is expanding today with Google Drive, Wallet, and even Gemini app integrations. more…
fullText:
Personal Intelligence in AI Mode is expanding today with Google Drive, Wallet, and even Gemini app integrations.

Before today’s announcement, Personal Intelligence in AI Mode supported Google Photos and Workspace (Gmail and Calendar). This is used to customize responses based on your data. The new Google Drive support lets AI Mode take into account your Docs, Sheets, and PDFs.

Following the Gemini app, Google Wallet integration is coming to AI Mode. On the safety front, AI Mode can only read information from your financial accounts. It cannot “move, manage, or invest your money.”

…you can map out your financial milestones and identify actionable ways to trim everyday spending. You can also maximize credit card benefits — like optimizing cash-back categories, travel perks, and reward points — based on your cards linked via Wallet.

The last integration today is the most interesting. You will be able to “securely connect your Gemini app to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode.”

	

…if you explore an idea in the Gemini app, AI Mode will have that foundation to build on, and vice versa.

This builds on the existing ability to have the Gemini app factor your Search history into answers. With this update, AI Mode can access “your Gemini chats, what you’ve shared with Gemini Apps (like photos, files, audio or video attachments, and screens you ask about), and associated insights and locations.” The option to make the connection is available today, but the feature will go live in the coming weeks.

You can control Personal Intelligence in AI Mode from this page.

Google will soon show a “Personalization” icon below tailored responses that lets you “view the context AI Mode uses.” 

The final update today will make AI Overviews and AI Mode responses “more personally relevant.”

So if you’ve been researching and planning for a trip, you can pick up right where you left off in a new search thread without starting over or repeating yourself. As always, you can adjust or turn off personalization at any time in your Search Settings.

title: The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is making its global debut today with huge preorder bonuses
snippet: The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max launch ushers the company into the world of cinema with an ARRI camera partnership and cutting-edge specs. more…
fullText:
The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max launch ushers the company into the world of cinema with an ARRI camera partnership and cutting-edge specs.

The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is Honor’s most cutting-edge flagship phone to date, and preorders for the global model begin today, November 24, 2026, starting in Malaysia. The phone goes for a retail price of RM5,999 and comes in Shadow Black, Glacier Silver, and Moss Green colorways. Preorders are available at Honor Experience Stores, on Honor Malaysia’s online store, and at a ton of official Honor shops across TikTok, Shopee, Lazada, and more, with further global availability to be announced soon.

Folks who preorder before the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max launch on December 4 will receive:

RM300 instant rebate

Professional Imaging Kit coupon (worth RM300)

FREE Harman Kardon Aura Studio 5 speaker (available exclusively during the pre-order period)

HONOR Magic9 Pro Max Magnetic Swap Case

Comprehensive protection and warranty coverage: 1-Year Liquid Damage Protection, 1-Year Screen Protection, 1-Year Back Cover Protection, 1-Year Extended Warranty and a 2-Year Battery Replacement service

3 months of complimentary Google AI Pro with 5TB of cloud storage

That’s a heck of a lot of bonuses. The Magic 9 Pro Max is Honor’s first phone to ship with ARRI camera licensing, and the company has been adamant that this is the most cutting-edge camera experience you’ll find on any smartphone to date. Honor’s phones have had great photography prowess, especially the Magic 7 and 8 series, but the Magic 9 Pro Max improves that with dual 200MP sensors, a fully overhauled video recording experience, and ARRI cinema modes.

	

The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max also ships with the Honor Imaging Chip H1, a first for the company, as it employs ARRI imaging-based AI algorithms into the RAW domain in real time. Honor also touts a class-leading CIPA 8.0 stabilization score for the 200MP telephoto camera and 200MP main camera, so shaky hands should still produce abundantly clear images and stable video.

The rest of the spec list reads mostly like a power user’s dream come true. It’s powered by a Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 SoC, 12GB of RAM with an additional 12GB of virtual RAM, an 8,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, 100W wired and 80W wireless charging, a third-gen Honor C3 RF chip, a 6.8-inch LTPO OLED display with anti-reflective coating, an anti-scratch NanoCrystal shield, 10,000 nits peak brightness, and 3840Hz PWM dimming. Plus, that fancy new design sports IP68, IP69, and IP69K water and dust-resistance ratings, and the whole thing ships with Magic OS 11 (based on Android 17).

title: Microsoft declares a Code Red in response to worst ever outage
snippet: The recent Microsoft 365 outage was the worst the service had ever experienced, with more than 80% of the company’s servers unresponsive at the worst point. The company has now declared a Code Red to address the way it prevents and responds to major failures in future. Microsoft has explained more about why it took so long to resolve the issue and said that it’s urgently working on new approaches to resolve any future incidents in less than an hour … more…
fullText:
The recent Microsoft 365 outage was the worst the service had ever experienced, with more than 80% of the company’s servers unresponsive at the worst point. The company has now declared a Code Red to address the way it prevents and responds to major failures in future.

Microsoft has explained more about why it took so long to resolve the issue and said that it’s urgently working on new approaches to resolve any future incidents in less than an hour …

Code Red is a common term used to describe the highest priority response to a major problem, pulling a significant number of engineers off their current tasks in order to maximize the resources applied to fixing it.

	

The senior execs responsible for the service told staff that it was the most customer-impacting incident ever experienced, and has acknowledged that not only was the problem itself unacceptable, but so too was the time taken to resolve it. Reuters got sight of a memo sent to the team.

It was the most ⁠customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to Silver’s memo.

One reason it took so long to work out what had happened was because the diagnostic data needed was “scattered across fragmented internal systems.” The memo says 11 separate Teams chats exchanged more than 11,000 messages as they struggled to work out what exactly had gone wrong.

Microsoft is now working on five interrelated approaches to achieve a target resolution time of less than an hour for any future incidents of this nature.

snippet: Following its debut on the Galaxy Watch 9 earlier this year, Samsung is finally rolling out Wear OS 7 to older Galaxy Watch models with its One UI 9 Watch update. more…
fullText:
Following its debut on the Galaxy Watch 9 earlier this year, Samsung is finally rolling out Wear OS 7 to older Galaxy Watch models with its One UI 9 Watch update.

Samsung’s One UI 9 Watch update is largely focused on new health features including Vitals, Heart Health Score, Daily Cardio Load, Fitness Index, and improvements to both Sleep Coaching and Sleep Apnea alerts. 

“Vitals” is perhaps the most useful day-to-day addition, with Samsung Health collecting data on key vital signs such as heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and blood oxygen and establishing a range so you can see when your vitals are out of the usual range. 

One UI 9 Watch is based on Wear OS 7, and also includes an improved Compass app with “Track Back,” a feature that helps users to follow their route back to a recorded point.

	

There’s also a new “Portrait Watch Face” that can adjust the clock face around the subject of a photo. 

Samsung is, as of today, officially rolling out One UI 9 Watch with Wear OS 7 to the Galaxy Watch 8 and Galaxy Watch 8 Classic. Meanwhile, the update is in beta for several other older models which will be updated soon including:

Galaxy Watch Ultra

Galaxy Watch 7

Galaxy Watch 6/Classic

The Galaxy Watch 5 series and Watch FE should also be getting the update, but no beta is available for those devices. Samsung’s first Wear OS watches, the Galaxy Watch 4 series, will not get the update.

title: New OpenAI and Anthropic models sound alarms on safety and control, report
snippet: Frontier AI models that have yet to be released by OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly reaching the point where employees believe they cannot be safely released or controlled, employees reportedly say. more…
fullText:
Frontier AI models that have yet to be released by OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly reaching the point where employees believe they cannot be safely released or controlled, employees reportedly say.

Axios cites “more than two dozen” employees inside of OpenAI and Anthropic who are sounding warnings around unreleased models from both companies. 

While both OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude public models are increasingly powerful, these employees say that new models behind the scenes are starting to beat out the technical solutions for controlling them. This has led to debates between those who think they’ll be able to fix these problems, and others who believe companies should stop training new models altogether due to the risks.

One researcher explains:

	

If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they’re actually smarter than us … they will in fact be able to trick us successfully. And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we’ve had at work up until now sort of go out the window.

The report goes out to point out that some researchers feel that executives at major AI companies have become “out of touch” with the severity of safety risks, though Axios was told that OpenAI is adopting new safety practices while Anthropic said that “Keeping a model internal doesn’t make it safe,” adding that “we may slow down or hold back even when it costs us.”

title: Anthropic launches new Claude Ship feature for builders
snippet: Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.” more…
fullText:
Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”

Claude Ship helps agentic coders build faster

Claude Ship is a new product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding. 

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic says. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

Three agents make up Claude Ship

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals. 

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

You can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here. 

Introducing Claude Ship (beta): Claude can review your pull requests, work on fixes, and approve the ones your team's policy allows.

The goal is to help you ship code as fast as you can write it. pic.twitter.com/b9OBAhEBmr

title: Nearly every major smartphone brand is slashing targets for 2027
snippet: According to a new report out of China, nearly every major smartphone brand is rethinking its shipment targets for 2027 and slashing its numbers, some by nearly 30%. more…
fullText:
According to a new report out of China, nearly every major smartphone brand is rethinking its shipment targets for 2027 and slashing its numbers, some by nearly 30%.

Jiemian News reports (via @jukan05) that nearly every major brand will be cutting back its forecasts for 2027 compared to 2026. This includes:

Samsung: 210 million, down 9.5%

Apple: 220 million, down 5.6%

Xiaomi: 90 million, down 25%

Oppo: 90 million, down 14%

Transsion: 66 million, down 12%

Vivo: 60 million, down 29%

Huawei: 50 million, down 16%

Lenovo/Motorola: 40 million, down 20%

These are just targets and subject to change, but they show that smartphone brands recognize that 2027 is going to be a much slower year amid the tight constraints of RAM, chip, and other component shortages and rising prices. Honor, notably, isn’t mentioned as the company is apparently aiming for the same 50 million units shipped as it was targeting in 2026 following a Q3 where it actually managed growth.

The cuts here largely impact mid-range and entry-level phones, as those are generally the biggest sellers in terms of sheer quantity, but also the devices most affected by rising production costs.

title: A month with the iPhone Duo has changed how I use my phone
snippet: From reading more books to breaking mindless scrolling habits, Apple's foldable has changed my daily routines in ways I didn't anticipate.
fullText:
For years, the definition of a premium smartphone depended on its cameras, processors, and how light it felt when you stowed it in your pocket. The iPhone Duo challenges that concept by asking consumers to pay more for a fundamentally different smartphone experience, even if it means sacrificing what they’ve long thought of as high-end features.

In a little under a month of using the Duo, I’ve found that the trade-offs I was initially concerned about matter far less to me than I had expected. What’s been more interesting is how the Duo’s foldable form factor has changed my everyday habits, including how I interact with apps, which apps I use, and how I organize and personalize the phone itself.

I also easily forgot a number of my initial concerns about switching to the Duo. The apps, for the most part, are now optimized for the Duo; I’ve reacquainted myself with Touch ID; and I don’t miss the Pro Max camera on most days.

That’s not to say the Duo doesn’t have its shortcomings. I still miss that telephoto lens sometimes, and I’m still longing for Face ID — though not as much since Apple shipped a face unlock feature in the latest update. But after a month of using the Duo, I’ve found these compromises have had less of an impact on my day-to-day experience compared with the benefits that the new form factor brings.

Multitasking feels more natural

I was surprised by how much I’ve grown to appreciate the Duo’s multitasking capabilities. Initially, I didn’t think I’d regularly use it to view two apps side by side, given the still fairly limited screen space even while the phone is unfolded, especially compared with an iPad. But I’ve found myself snapping apps to both halves of the screen more often than I had imagined.

For starters, Apple has made this side-by-side mode incredibly intuitive and easy to use — you simply drag the app over to the left or right side of the screen and drop it into the target box that appears.

I have regularly taken advantage of this feature to do all sorts of things. 

Image Credits:Apple

I really enjoy keeping X open as I read through the news, which allows me to switch back and forth between the article I’m reading and real-time reactions to it. Sometimes I’ll keep email or Slack open on the side while I’m working on something else so I don’t miss an important message or notification.

And much like the overstimulated members of Gen Z (which I am not), I sometimes like scrolling social media while engaging with some other media off to the side. 

Case in point: I passively watched Netflix’s “Love is Blind” reunion while reading the gossipy tweets and Reddit posts about the main characters on the other side of the screen. This sort of TV watching behavior used to be called second-screen viewing, but now it’s morphing into something new. Everything is happening on one screen, so should we call it “Duo screen viewing,” perhaps? It makes me long for even more interactive TV experiences where commentary and content are combined.

It really is like having two phones

I’ve noticed another shift in my behavior since adopting the Duo as my main device. When I’m out and about, the Duo feels more like an (arguably heavier) iPhone mini. For those who still miss smaller iPhones, the Duo is the next best thing. Despite its weight, the phone feels small. You can cover it with one hand; you can type with a thumb; you can reach the top and bottom easily; and you can even fit it into your front and back pockets. The Pro Max now feels unbelievably strange in my hand — how was I ever comfortable wrangling this giant rectangle?

The Duo’s small screen works well when you’re on the go, especially for short interactions like responding to a quick text or pulling up directions to a destination. It’s not as great for mindless scrolling, which I appreciate, as it forces me to engage with the real world instead of killing every moment of boredom or unease by opening up apps.

An illustration of the Apple iPhone Duo is displayed at a store in Krakow, Poland, on October 27, 2026. (Photo by Karolina Janik/JPix/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Image Credits:NurPhoto / Contributor (opens in a new window) / Getty Images

But when you’re home or somewhere with time to kill, you can unfold the screen and enjoy your apps super-sized. It’s the best of both worlds.

I find that I instinctively unfold the phone when I’m preparing to watch videos, because the larger screen is best for that. It’s also unfolded if I’m shopping, as it’s more convenient for looking at products, zooming in to examine the details, or complete checkout forms.

Generally, I also unfold the Duo when I’m actively using apps. This setup has also allowed me to rethink my Home Screen layout: With the Duo closed, I prefer to see just widgets on the small screen with key information like weather, time, battery life, and so on. Meanwhile, the only app icons on the Home Screen are those in the dock.

The Duo apps are ready now

In the weeks since its launch, most of the apps that weren’t yet optimized for the Duo have been upgraded to support its foldable form factor. In mid-November, Apple said there were over 200,000 Duo-ready apps, and in my experience, that certainly feels true. A majority of my so-called “daily drivers” — with the glaring exception of key Google apps like Gmail and Drive — have dropped the black band on the side of the screen that was frustrating early testers of the phone.

Most apps now take advantage of the available space, whether that’s on the Duo’s small front screen or the wider, unfolded one.

I’ve also found it interesting to see the different interpretations developers have had for how to best optimize their app for Duo. 

Some have used the form factor as a way to bring in some sort of novelty: there’s a note-taking app that opens and closes like a notebook, with pages you can write on with the Apple Pencil; a retro Walkman-like music player; a tiny typewriter; a gaming handheld; a game where you close the phone to make grilled cheese.

Image Credits:Tiny Computers

As much as I love the whimsy of this group of apps, I appreciate how my everyday apps feel better to use on the unfolded screen. Spotify, at last, feels less cluttered when it has more screen real estate. A number of note-taking, list-making, and calendar apps also feel somehow more usable when spread out.

The Netflix app is actually fantastic with its support for multiple viewing modes, which include playing video on the closed outer display, the “laptop” orientation with its big player controls, and the “tent” mode. 

Image Credits:Apple

Other developers have similarly reimagined how their app would work if it had originally been designed for the Duo’s small and larger screens. 

One good example of this is Sofa, a handy utility for organizing the books, movies, TV shows, podcasts, albums, and games you want to check out. When the Duo is closed, its navigation is tucked off to the right side in a vertical bar, while the main screen focuses on the items you’ve saved. But when the Duo is unfolded, the number of items displayed on the screen also expands into a two-column layout, with more of your items featured on the screen and your lists on the left side. It doesn’t feel like two different apps, but like you’ve opened up the app itself and given it more space to spread out.

Image Credits:Sofa (screenshot from their Threads post) (opens in a new window)

In terms of your daily social media scroll, apps like TikTok and Instagram have been updated to be perfectly usable on the Duo, whether the phone is open or closed. When closed, TikTok now stretches the video to cover the screen, instead of showing the ugly black bar. Scrolling short-form videos on the Duo, while unfolded like a slightly smaller iPad mini, has become my preferred way to watch.

Image Credits:TikTok screenshot from folded Duo

I’m reading more books

Here’s another surprise: I’ve spent less time with my Kindle, and am instead reading books on my Duo. Unfolded, the Duo is a decent enough replacement for an e-book reader, albeit it can be a bit more stimulating as it’s not an e-ink device. However, the matte inner screen isn’t quite as bright and distracting as your typical glossy OLED display. There’s less glare and softer reflections, but there’s also something about the display that just feels calmer than a smartphone, allowing you to more fully engage with a book’s text.

Unfolded and held vertically, reading on the Duo feels a lot like reading on the standard Kindle, at least in terms of hand-feel. And putting your phone into the “Do Not Disturb” focus mode can help you not be distracted by incoming notifications and messages while you read. 

Image Credits:Actually Read (opens in a new window)

You can also unfold the device while keeping it in landscape orientation, with the screens bent slightly inward like a real book. For even more fun, you can turn on Kindle’s page-turn animation, which makes it seem as if you’re turning the page in a physical book. And I love how you can “performatively read” using an app like Book2Life or Actually Read — they display the book’s cover on the Duo’s outer screen as you read the text on the inner screen.

E-book readers will likely find they can carry one less device when they’re out and about, because the Duo can stand in for whatever Kindle or other reader you typically keep in your purse or bag. You can save the Kindle for other times, whether that’s at home, on long travel days, or when you don’t want to worry about sand getting into your $2,000 phone.

I don’t need a PopSocket

On the big-screened iPhone 17 Pro Max I used to carry, I tended to keep a PopSocket of some sort on the back because the phone was both heavy and large, which made it hard to hold for longer periods of time. The Duo is similarly heavy, but its shape makes it far easier to hold in one hand without the extra help.

Folded, you can do the usual one-handed hold where the bottom edge of the phone rests on your pinky, your other three fingers cradle the back, and your thumb is free to navigate the screen. 

Unfolded, the Duo’s like using a small Kindle or iPad mini, where two hands are required. You also don’t need a PopSocket for balancing the phone on the side, because it can be propped up like a tent or opened like a tiny laptop. Or, if you prefer, Apple and others offer Duo cases with a built-in stand. (Apple’s case comes in navy and taupe, though, so if you’re not boring, you’ll probably want to shop from third-party vendors).

ScreenshotImage Credits:PopSockets (opens in a new window)

If you think you still might need a PopSocket at times, or you just aren’t ready to give it up, the brand now makes a slimmer version: its Low-Pro Grip. There are other competitors, like the OhSnap grips, which aren’t a bad alternative either.  

It’s inspiring personalization

There’s something about the Duo that seems to have kicked off a new iPhone personalization trend, at least judging by what I’ve been seeing on social media.

Unlike a regular iPhone, where every phone case is simply a shell that offers a degree of protection based on the materials used, the Duo case lineup provides far more variety. 

You can buy cases with and without built-in screen protectors, and some use adhesive to better stick to the outer screen, while others don’t. Some cases let you customize the band around the outer screen with a different color than the case that protects the rest of the phone.

Then you have cases that cover the hinge, while others leave it exposed. There are cases that offer holes where you can attach straps, wristlets, and charms. Some of those have attachment points at the bottom and others on the side.

Essentially, there are a lot of options for customizing how you want to carry the Duo and how you want to express your own style.

I’m also now starting to see whimsical cases that come with attached pens. (Thank goodness — most of the pen cases so far have been kind of plain!)

Image Credits:Kai Studio (opens in a new window)

I also believe there’s something about the Duo that particularly appeals to women. Maybe because it’s small, or maybe it’s because you can attach a strap to its side and carry it like a little purse. Or maybe because, like a purse, you can deck it out with chains and charms — a choice that’s grown increasingly popular as young people have embraced whimsical, retro tech as a way to express their individuality and sense of fashion.

The Duo easily lends itself to this trend, perhaps even more than a regular iPhone. It becomes an accessory you want on display, not one buried in a bag.  

Image Credits:Cases.com (opens in a new window)

Before switching to the Duo, I spent a lot of time thinking about what I’d be giving up by moving away from the Pro Max. 

I’m surprised to find that, a month later, I only think about what I’d have to give up if I switched back to a traditional iPhone. It’s not just the extra space of the unfolded screen I’d miss — it’s all the little habits I’ve developed around having different screen sizes for different purposes. 

The Duo makes me pause and think about how I want to use an app. That small moment of deliberation, before I even open the phone, has helped me break some of my more mindless smartphone habits, particularly around social media.

That’s not a benefit I could have anticipated if I’d judged the device by its specifications alone.

title: Tidal Will Reject and Remove Music That Is 100% AI
snippet: The streaming app says it’s being flooded with AI-generated tracks.
fullText:
The flood is too much for Tidal. The music streaming app announced on Tuesday that it is banning all tracks it determines to be entirely AI-generated. The platform said it’s making the move after being increasingly inundated with non-human music. As of Dec. 9, Tidal will no longer accept or host fully AI-generated tracks.

The app also said distributors, such as DistroKid, TuneCore, CD Baby and others,  would not be allowed to deliver wholly AI-generated music.

According to Tidal, 43% of tracks distributed to the app over the past three months were completely AI-generated, including 60% of the music submitted on Nov. 6 alone. Tidal said the affected tracks were labeled as AI and removed from the royalty pool, which is the pot of subscription and ad revenue paid out to rights holders.

			

More from CNET

Before Tuesday’s action, Tidal had tried to lessen AI’s influence by identifying, labeling and demonetizing AI tracks, as outlined in its AI policy. But amid the growing influx of AI music, representatives for the app said it was time for “a more drastic change.”

Tidal said there are 27 million tracks in its catalog that are 100% AI, but 96% of them have not been streamed at all in the past three months. Those 27 million tracks make up 6.3% of Tidal’s entire listings.

AI music “diverts streams and royalties away from the artists and confuses fans,” Tidal said in a statement.  “At this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried.”

The company has removed more than 65,000 tracks flagged for artist-name impersonation.

Some AI help is permitted. Musical tracks where the maker used AI assistance  but did not rely on it to generate the entire track will be allowed on the platform. Tidal uses ⁠Ircam Amplify to detect AI.

A Tidal representative told CNET that the app does not set a maximum amount of AI assistance that can be used to make tracks, and affirmed that only tracks that are deemed 100% AI-generated would be removed.

The spokesperson also said that most complaints about AI music on Tidal concerned impersonation and copyright infringement.

Read more: I Only Listened to AI Music for a Week. It Was Terrible, but Not for the Reason You Think

“Tidal will always fight for artists to get paid more,” the company said in its announcement. “Everything in this update comes back to that. If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for or copied by someone pretending to be you.”

Slop music is all too easy to create

Generating music with AI is increasingly easy with online tools. The AI song-generation platform Suno can create songs using only text prompts. With Google’s Lyria, you can use photos or text prompts to generate tracks up to 3 minutes long.

It’s not illegal to create AI music and distribute it to streaming apps. Creators can’t legally clone the voice or likeness of real artists, nor can they violate copyright laws by copying the same lyrics and melodies. Creators also must follow the terms of service of the various streaming apps they distribute to.

AI music also is not just about creating hit songs. Some industries need affordable music for short-form videos, games, apps and retail spaces, and they are increasingly turning to AI to supply it.

But streaming apps and other companies are fighting back against AI slop, which refers to often poor-quality AI-generated social media posts, articles, music, videos and images inundating the internet in an attempt to generate click-and-stream revenue.

YouTube recently rolled out a new labeling system to indicate which music is AI-generated. Deezer provides a free tool listeners can use to see which tracks are AI-generated. Spotify is labeling which musicians are AI and which are human. Apple is flagging AI-generated music so listeners can spot it.

title: I Tried Using Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots to Save on Groceries. They’re Not Quite There Yet
snippet: I tried using AI agents to build me the cheapest grocery order possible. They exhibited a startling lack of curiosity and autonomous thinking.
fullText:
High grocery prices have been in the news for years now. The cost of eggs, how much you’re paying for a bowl of cereal and whether or not meat is back on the menu are the recurring subjects of nationwide headlines.

So before you drop a fortune on gas and drive out to the grocery store to spend even more on sustenance in your prep for hosting or bringing dishes to your holiday celebrations, you might consider using an AI agent to find you the best deal possible. 

Although, in my experience, it’s not as simple as the AI marketing makes it sound. Here’s what happened when I tried to use AI agents to find the lowest possible prices on groceries.

			

More from CNET

Taking an inventory

AI agents such as Meta Muse and ChatGPT’s Dots can only crawl so many sites and online fliers for prices. Some stores and e-commerce sites have blocked AI agents from accessing their URLs. The first step in finding cheaper groceries with AI agents is to check which sites and stores they can access for price comparisons. 

Where both agents missed a step was in the limitations they put on their searches, at first only looking at the retailers I had shown via my receipts and a few other big-name grocery stores. 

I clarified in the chats and in a 20-minute voice conversation with Muse and a 14-minute voice conversation with Dots that they should expand their horizons and look at discount online retailers like Martie.com, and check what they could around advertised pricing and offerings at local farmers’ markets.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Meta Muse

Muse stuck to the basics like Ralphs, Target and Walmart, and then expanded to Sprouts, Vons and Martie.com when prompted. 

After further nudging, Muse also reviewed user-reported pricing from Costco (I don’t have a membership), gave me vague information about Grocery Outlet, suggested Misfits Market/Imperfect Foods, ruled out Amazon Fresh and gave me some sample pricing from a local butcher for meats. 

Muse also checked some local bakery prices after I mentioned I’d like to find alternatives to sweet treats at a more affordable price.

ChatGPT Dots

Dots checked all the usual places that Meta Muse checked with a few extras thrown in — Smart & Final for produce, meat and some packaged products, and Super King’s monthly ad.

Neither of the tools checked Trader Joe’s. Muse said that the grocery chain doesn’t show prices of its products online, despite me finding that the Trader Joe’s website shows prices of its products online. Both Dots and Muse admitted to only checking the local store’s pages when asked.

Receipts as a starting point

You could spend some time making a list from scratch of all the groceries you might need every two weeks and give that list to the AI agent for its search. You could also skip all that and take some pics of your most recent grocery receipts and online payments and have the AI agent build the list itself. 

I had some receipts saved, and the AI agents I used for this test were able to put together an accurate grocery list from them. I also provided emails showing receipts from online orders of household items and groceries for the past month to build my orders.

Meta Muse

Muse took my receipts and concluded that, surprise, surprise, shopping at Gelson’s was not as cost-effective as shopping at Walmart. It spat out a lot of specific information about comparisons on some of the items in my list, but completely ignored others. 

ChatGPT Dots

Dots looked over my receipts and recommended I try shopping at Super King for most fresh meat, produce and a few grains, and keep Walmart as my main option for packaged products like pasta sauce. 

No grocery lists from either

Both tools tackled this task in a way I was not expecting — as a narrative exploration of my overall grocery spending, with generalized suggestions supported by specific examples of spot pricing. 

It was kind of like they’ve been optimized to write essays about grocery shopping as a school assignment, and not to be agentic personal assistants for real-world work.

Maybe it was the way I phrased the task, but I was hoping to get an actual shopping list with price comparisons for each item, or at least equivalent items, and a guide on where and how to procure said items. 

Neither AI agent provided this autonomously and had to be directly prompted to provide grocery lists in response to a very specific request.

Perks of a personal shopper

AI agents are supposed to be pros at anticipating the needs of their human bosses. I was keen to see how the always-on AI agents would handle managing the recurring needs of a small household and if they might make any autonomous suggestions meant to save me money in ways I hadn’t anticipated. 

Meta Muse

At no point did Muse seem to be actually thinking outside the strict parameters of the review of the items on the receipts I sent. This felt more like a conversation about what I’d previously purchased with a side serving of attempts to get me to connect Instacart to the tool.

It was also the most confusing grocery shopping experience I have ever had. That might be on me, but I would assume the agent might ask some questions, like how often I usually shop, what my monthly budget for groceries is, and how many people and animals live in the house. Muse didn’t ask any of those things and had to be prompted consistently.

Muse sent me the final grocery list as a raw Markdown file, which was hilarious. I got a .pdf version after explicitly asking for one. 

My original total with one in-person shop and one online order was about $180. Muse’s total with three in-person shops and one online order came in at around $153.

ChatGPT Dots

Dots was slightly better suited to this task after some prodding, and gave me some options for building prep meals with low-effort, high-protein recipes based on how I usually shop. 

Dots’ final grocery list included everything I asked for, but still missed some key items, like solid substitutes for pricey prepped foods. Dot’s final total with two in-person shopping trips and a whole lot of missing items came out to around $85.

My overall experience of using AI agents for grocery shopping

This test reinforced my findings about how agentic AI tools tackle domestic or traditionally invisible labor tasks. In my limited use cases so far, they are about as useful as a loose dog turd tumbling around in a clothes dryer. 

If you’re not looking to book a flight and hotel for a business conference in Philadelphia or put your Sweetgreen order on autopilot, the AI agents exhibit a startling lack of curiosity and autonomous thinking. 

There’s still a large gap in common sense on the part of agentic AI for those of us hoping these tools will make our everyday lives outside of a 9-to-5 easier, more affordable or less hectic. I hope that changes as they learn.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Rachel Kane
						

						

							Contributor and former Senior Editor						
					

											

								

											Rachel is a freelancer based in Echo Park, Los Angeles and has been writing and producing content for nearly two decades on subjects ranging from tech to fashion, health and lifestyle to entertainment and education. She's currently a Professor of Practice at Arizona State University's Walter Cronkite School of Journalism and Mass Communication, helping to mold the new minds who will inherit the media landscape. She's hoping to prevent the singularity by being polite to chatbots and spends way too much time refining Midjourney prompts.

title: Nothing Ear (note) is yet another AI recorder, but with earbuds inside
snippet: Set to launch on December 8, Nothing has confirmed its mysterious AI product will be called “Ear (note),” and it’s an AI recorder with earbuds inside. more…
fullText:
Set to launch on December 8, Nothing has confirmed its mysterious AI product will be called “Ear (note),” and it’s an AI recorder with earbuds inside.

Update 11/25: Nothing has shared another image of Ear (note), showing how the case opens and the earbuds inside. The company adds that the audio quality matches Nothing’s “best in-ear audio experience,” explaining:

Ear (note) is a new approach to personal productivity, making it easy to transcribe, summarise and act on in-person conversations, calls, online meetings and thoughts – without requiring an additional device or new behaviours. At the same time, Ear (note) doesn’t compromise on audio, combining Hi-Res Audio and high-quality audio capture with AI that works in the background.

Introducing a new form factor, this is also the most evolved version of Nothing’s transparent design language. Built around an aluminium case with squared edges and a cool metallic finish, Ear (note) introduces machined metal and brutalist forms into Nothing’s transparent design language. Clear windows are inspired by the contours of topographic maps, revealing depth and dimensionality within the case. The TALK button and a new RECORD button draw on the controls on a retro Walkman, both positioned to be easy to reach and to provide tactile feedback when activated.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Nothing has confirmed that its new AI product is “Ear (note).” This builds on a pair of earbuds by turning the charging case into an AI-powered recorder.

The case has a “Talk” button, like Ear (3), which can be used to record your own voice, where a record button enables the ability to “record and transcribe conversations.” Ear (3a)’s ability to record audio from the earbuds will also carry over to Ear (note), giving the product the ability to record both conversations in person and over the phone. 

	

Nothing is entering a crowded market here with products from Plaud, Amazon, and countless others already offering AI recording/transcribing products, but building in earbuds is indeed a unique selling point. 

Nothing Ear (note) is launching on December 8, though pricing is unclear. Pei’s comments suggest a subscription will be used in some capacity.

title: South Korea proceeds with case over allegedly misleading Apple Intelligence ads [U]
snippet: South Korea’s Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) announced today that it has opened formal proceedings against Apple over its advertising of Apple Intelligence features for the iPhone 16 lineup. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
South Korea’s Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) announced today that it has opened formal proceedings against Apple over its advertising of Apple Intelligence features for the iPhone 16 lineup. Here are the details.

A bit of background

Back in March 2025, shortly after Apple announced it was delaying the rollout of what would eventually become Siri AI, the South Korean civic group Seoul YMCA filed a complaint with the KFTC.

At the time, Yonhap reported that the organization had previously called on Apple to compensate affected customers, and alleged that the company may have continued to market the iPhone 16 lineup despite already knowing that some of its advertised AI features would be delayed.

As 9to5Mac readers will likely remember, Apple widely advertised Apple Intelligence and AI-powered Siri features as part of its iPhone 16 launch campaign, going so far as to give its iconic Fifth Avenue store an Apple Intelligence-themed makeover and run an ad campaign starring Bella Ramsey.

This landed Apple in legal and regulatory trouble in multiple markets, including the US, where the company agreed to a $250 million class action settlement earlier this year, and Brazil, where it came under scrutiny from a consumer protection agency in May. Now, the company is facing potential penalties in South Korea as well.

Apple faces potential penalties in South Korea

As a result of Seoul YMCA’s complaint, the KFTC conducted an investigation into Apple’s advertising practices. Today, the regulator announced (via MacRumors) that its investigators had submitted their findings and recommendations for formal deliberation by the Commission.

According to the KFTC’s press release, investigators concluded that Apple advertised Apple Intelligence and its planned staggered rollout on the iPhone 16 website, but “concealed, downplayed, or omitted information material to consumers’ purchasing decisions.”

That included, per the press release (translation ours):

The fact that some of the nine Apple Intelligence features would be difficult to deliver in US English by the end of 2024, and when those features would become available.

The fact that some features were not available in US English as of October 2024.

The fact that some features would be difficult to deliver in Korean by early April 2025, and when those features would become available.

The press release also notes that Genmoji, Image Playground, “Siri with the ability to understand personal context,” and “Siri that provides step-by-step guidance” were not made available as advertised:

For example, Siri’s ability to understand personal context was advertised as being scheduled to launch first in US English by the end of 2024, as currently available in US English in October 2024, and as scheduled to support Korean in early April 2025.

In reality, the feature was not launched in US English until September 2026, with Korean language support following in October 2026.

As a result, the investigators concluded that Apple’s conduct constituted a violation of the country’s Labeling and Advertising Act, which prohibits deceptive labeling and advertising.

They recommended issuing corrective orders, including a prohibition on such conduct in the future, as well as imposing a financial penalty.

They also estimate that Apple’s revenue associated with the alleged violation amounts to approximately 3.35 trillion South Korean won (roughly $2.5 billion), though the KFTC’s press release does not specify the amount of the fine.

⁠Yonhap noted today that the fine could reach roughly $48 million, while ⁠KBS reported that it could range between $21 million and $42 million.

With the report now submitted, Apple has six weeks to submit its written defense before the Commission deliberates and makes a final determination on whether the company violated the law and, if so, how much it should be fined.

Update, November 27, 12:08 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

At Apple, we deeply value the relationship with our customers in Korea and have always focused on delivering the best products and services in the world. Since we added Korean language support for Apple Intelligence last year, users have benefited from dozens of powerful features that are integrated across Apple’s platforms. And we have continued to build on that commitment with the recent launch of Korean language support for Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that’s more capable, conversational, and personal. We have cooperated with the KFTC’s investigation and disagree with the conclusions in the Examiner’s Report. We look forward to presenting a fulsome defense before the Commission.

title: Best Black Friday E-Bike and Electric Scooter Deals: Save Up to $1,100
snippet: From everyday commuter e-bikes to high-performance scooters and beginner-friendly electric unicycles, here are some of the best Black Friday deals on rides I’ve tested or currently have in-house for review.
fullText:
If you’ve been thinking about buying an electric bike, scooter or electric unicycle, Black Friday and Cyber Monday are bringing some good opportunities to save. Segway, Apollo, Inmotion and several other manufacturers have marked down their rides, with discounts ranging from $100 to more than $1,000.

I’ve had several of these models in-house for testing, from everyday commuters to bikes capable of carrying passengers and cargo. Some also offer features riders will appreciate, including automatic lighting, turn signals, Apple Find My support and rear-approach detection.

Saving money shouldn’t mean compromising on safety. That’s why I’m focusing on models with UL-certified electrical systems, specifically UL 2849 for e-bikes and UL 2272 for electric scooters and unicycles. Read more about battery safety and proper charging.

With all of that in mind, here are the Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals worth checking out.

			

More from CNET

Segway Myon: $1,600 (Save $400)

Regular price: $2,000

The Segway Myon is one of the newer commuter e-bikes I’ve tried. It has a 500-watt motor, 85 Newton-meter of torque and pedal assistance up to 28 miles per hour. There’s also Apple Find My support, automatic lighting and Segway’s AirLock system, which can unlock the bike as you approach. You can also add the optional Rearview Radar for $100 to receive alerts about vehicles approaching from behind.

At $400 off, it’s worth considering if you’re looking for an everyday commuter with some useful technology built in.

Segway Muxi Pro: $1,800 (Save $200)

Regular price: $2,000

The Segway Muxi Pro is designed for carrying passengers and cargo, and I’ve been testing its practicality for everyday family use, including transporting my young son. The bike has automatic lighting, integrated turn signals and Apple Find My support, which can help locate the bike if it goes missing. It also includes the $100 Rearview Radar option.

The Muxi is an interesting alternative for errands and shorter trips where you might otherwise grab the car.

Segway Xyber Air: $1,800 (Save $200)

Regular price: $2,000

The Segway Xyber Air is another Segway I’ve tested, but this one is more about recreational riding than commuting or hauling groceries. Its moto-inspired design gives it a different look from your typical e-bike, and it supports Apple Find My, adding another layer of security when it’s parked.

Segway has additional deals on the Xafari and Xyber, with advertised savings reaching $1,300.

Shop all Segway Black Friday deals.

Aventon Current ADV: $3,999 (Free Fast Charger)

Regular price: $3,999 | Free charger valued at $259

The Aventon Current ADV isn’t discounted, but Aventon is including a fast charger valued at $259. I’ve tested this full-suspension electric mountain bike in-house. It has a mid-drive motor producing up to 120Nm of torque and a claimed maximum range of 105 miles. It also offers GPS-based security features, including location tracking and an alarm system. Even though it’s an e-mountain bike, I love how it handles New York’s bumpy streets.

Aventon has additional discounts of up to $200 on select Aventure, Level and Pace models.

Shop all Aventon Black Friday deals.

Best Black Friday electric scooter deals

Apollo Dash: $529 (Save $170)

Regular price: $699

The Apollo Dash is aimed at first-time scooter riders who want something practical without spending a fortune. It weighs 43 pounds, folds in about three seconds and has a claimed range of up to 25 miles. It also supports Apple Find My, a useful feature if your scooter ever goes missing.

I have the Dash in-house, but since I’m above its rated rider weight, my son and partner are handling the riding portion of the testing under my guidance. I’ll have more to share in a full hands-on review.

Apollo Go Stellar: $1,099 (Save $100)

Regular price: $1,199

The Apollo Go Stellar offers a step up in performance with dual motors, a top speed of up to 32 mph and a claimed range of 38 miles. At 55 pounds, it’s heavier than the Dash but adds dual-spring suspension and Apple Find My support. It’s another scooter on my testing list. 

Apollo Phantom 2.0: $1,999 (Save $500)

Regular price: $2,499

For riders looking for considerably more power, the Apollo Phantom 2.0 has dual motors, a top speed of up to 44 mph and a claimed range of 50 miles. It also features regenerative braking, dual-spring suspension, an IP66 water-resistance rating and Apple Find My support.

At 102 pounds, however, this isn’t a scooter you’ll want to carry up several flights of stairs.

Apollo also has discounts on its City lineup and higher-performance Phantom Stellar.

Shop all Apollo scooter deals.

Segway Max G3 Plus: $1,000 (Save $500)

Regular price: $1,500

The Segway Max G3 Plus is another scooter we’ve had in-house. It has a claimed range of up to 56 miles, front and rear hydraulic suspension, 11-inch self-sealing tires, disc brakes and integrated turn signals. It also has Segway’s traction control system and electronic braking assistance.

At $500 off, it’s worth considering if you’re looking for something with more performance and comfort than a basic commuter scooter. I’ll have more to share about my experience with it in an upcoming hands-on review.

Vmax VX2 Hub: $959 (Save $640)

Regular price: $1,599

The Vmax VX2 Hub is one of the more powerful single-motor scooters we’ve tested, with 1,900 watts of peak power and an advertised top speed of 34 mph. What impressed me was how well it handled my weight, especially considering its relatively modest size. At $640 off, it’s worth considering if you’re looking for a compact scooter with some serious power.

Vmax VX2 Lite: $639 (Save $460)

Regular price: $1,099

The Vmax VX2 Lite is another scooter on my review list. It’s a more affordable alternative to the Hub, and at $460 off, it could be worth checking out if you don’t need the Hub’s additional performance. I’ll have more to share once I’ve had a chance to test it.

Best Black Friday electric unicycle deals

Inmotion V9: $799 (Save $500)

Regular price: $1,299

The Inmotion V9 is one of the more beginner-friendly electric unicycles I’ve reviewed. It has built-in cellular connectivity, allowing you to track its location if it goes missing, along with suspension for a more comfortable ride. It’s also UL 2272 certified, an important consideration when bringing a lithium-ion-powered ride into your home.

At $500 off, it’s an appealing option for anyone looking to get into electric unicycles without spending a fortune.

Shop Inmotion’s Black Friday deals.

More Black Friday e-bike deals

If none of these models fit your needs, there are a few other sales worth checking out.

Super73: Save up to $600

Super73 has discounts on select models, including the Z Miami Core and S2 Laguna, both priced at $1,895. Its sale runs through Dec. 2.

Velotric: Save up to $700

Velotric is offering savings of up to $700 on select e-bikes, including the Summit 1, advertised at $1,299. The Nomad 2 and folding Fold 1 Plus are also discounted.

Juiced Bikes: Save up to $445 on Scrambler e-bikes

Juiced Bikes has marked down several models in its Scrambler lineup for Black Friday. The Scrambler Mini starts at $949, down from $1,164, while the Scrambler Hardtail is $1,599 (save $445) and the Full Suspension is $1,799 (save $445). If you’re looking for more range, the dual-battery Hardtail is $1,899, down from $2,344.

Shop Juiced Bikes Black Friday deals.

More deals from these manufacturers

Segway also has discounts on several other scooters, including the Max G2 for $598.48, ZT3 Pro for $790 and E3 Pro for $500.

Many of the manufacturers featured here have additional Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals across their product lines. I wanted to spotlight the bikes, scooters and electric unicycles we’ve had or currently have in-house because we’ve actually spent time with them. There are other products we’ve tested that could have made this list, too, but I wanted to give readers a useful selection rather than overwhelm them with every discounted model.

Before you buy

Don’t get too caught up in the discount. Make sure the bike, scooter or unicycle fits your needs, particularly when it comes to rider weight, range, portability and storage. Manufacturers’ range estimates are generally based on favorable conditions, and your actual mileage will vary depending on weight, speed, hills and temperature.

Apple Find My and other tracking systems can help locate a missing ride, but they’re no substitute for a good physical lock. And when it comes to battery safety, look for the appropriate UL certification, use the manufacturer-approved charger and never charge your bike or scooter where it blocks your exit.

Most of these deals run through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, although some promotions continue into December. Prices and availability can change.

title: PrismML’s Bonsai 2.5 brings better coding and tool use to on-device AI
snippet: Back in July, PrismML claimed its roughly 4 GB, 1-bit Bonsai 27B was the first AI model of its size to run on an iPhone. Now PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an update to the model it introduced in September. more…
fullText:
Back in July, PrismML claimed its roughly 4 GB, 1-bit Bonsai 27B was the first AI model of its size to run on an iPhone. Now PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an update to the model it introduced in September.

The startup also drew attention when CEO Babak Hassibi told CNBC that Apple was evaluating its technology, as we reported at the time.

The new model is based on Qwen3.8 27B and keeps the same 5.9 GB footprint in its most compact format. This time, PrismML focused on helping the model handle longer tasks, including figuring out what to do when a tool returns an unexpected result or a step fails.

Bonsai 2.5 improved on six of the seven benchmarks PrismML highlights. Its SWE-bench Verified coding score rose from 60.8 to 75.6, while its AppWorld tool-use score jumped from 51.2 to 90.5. LiveCodeBench v6 dipped from 83.8 to 83.0.

What could that look like on a Mac? A coding assistant could inspect a private project, make a change, run the tests, and use the results to revise its fix. A document app could summarize a folder of sensitive files while keeping the processing on the device.

PrismML says Bonsai 2.5 runs on Mac, iPhone, and iPad through MLX. Its Apple silicon package is about 8.9 GB, and the model card walks through setup on a Mac. The weights are available for free under Apache 2.0.

For a closer look at how the model was compressed and tested, read PrismML’s technical white paper.

title: Nvidia proves it’s too big to fail
snippet: Good morning. Today I’m deciding whether the final Avengers: Doomsday trailer passes the “people just standing around” test, trying the new Material 3 Expressive Claude app on my Android devices, and stocking up on discounted XTEINK e-readers for Christmas gifts. more…
fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m deciding whether the final Avengers: Doomsday trailer passes the “people just standing around” test, trying the new Material 3 Expressive Claude app on my Android devices, and stocking up on discounted XTEINK e-readers for Christmas gifts.

Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Eleven days after leaving Nvidia, Jensen Huang is back as president, CEO, and a board director. The board voted unanimously to reinstate him on Monday, saying it was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead following a series of meetings. It also said input from senior levels of the US government left it confident that his reinstatement poses no national security risk.

	

I didn’t see this coming. Huang was dishonest to the public and to his board. He admitted to having affairs not only with an alleged Chinese spy, but also with an employee who directly reported to him. He is accused of facilitating the sale of Nvidia AI chips to companies like Megaspeed that knowingly purchased them with the intention of smuggling them into China, a contravention of US trade restrictions.

As recently as November 17th, the board chair, Harvey Jones, reiterated that the company had no intention of bringing back Huang as CEO. But things changed quickly on Sunday as President Trump reportedly reassured the board that Huang’s reinstatement posed no security risk to US intelligence, something that the new Democratic-led Congress will be sure to test via repeated subpoenas in the new year.

As Huang walked into the atrium at Nvidia’s headquarters, staff gathered around to cheer his return, and he addressed the crowd by saying he would be a “better CEO the second time around,” as if 11 days of unemployment had given him sufficient time to evaluate his past behavior.

Nvidia’s stock was up over 30% on Monday, rebounding from a disastrous end to last week that wiped out $4 trillion in Nasdaq value. It’s hard not to see Huang’s return as a direct response to this short-term disruption, which also hinted at a much more serious correction in the stock market. Nvidia’s stock had already fallen 24% between the day Huang resigned and Friday’s crunch, and with looming regulation from Congress in 2027, a rudderless AI industry could have been disastrous for the US economy writ large.

Though things may appear to be back to normal, or as normal as possible given the insanity of the past couple of weeks, Huang has returned to a very different trade environment. While he was away, Nvidia’s board formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to investigate whether the company’s actions violated any US embargoes. And as part of Huang’s return, Nvidia has committed to hiring its first chief compliance officer, an executive who will ostensibly not report directly to the CEO.

I was pretty gobsmacked when I saw the news of Huang’s return come across the wire at 9am ET yesterday. I’m still wrapping my head around it. Is Nvidia too big to fail, or just a symptom of a larger interdependency between the US executive branch and Big Tech? Huang promises to be a better leader this time around, but to whom: his employees, his customers, or his shareholders? Because he appears to be a very different person to each of those groups.

Google’s 3D emoji has wild Android spec requirements: 10GB of free space, 6GB RAM. Most Android phones have these specs now, so I disagree that the requirements are “wild.” But do we really need emoji that go this hard?

🛍️ Black Friday: the deals worth a look

Since it’s Black Friday week, I figured I’d round up some of the best deals we’ve found so far.

The gaming-tablet deal: The Legion Tab Gen 5 at $599 makes much more sense than it did at $899: an 8.8-inch 165Hz display, a 12GB/256GB configuration, and an included folio. It’s a good fit for someone specifically seeking a compact Android gaming machine.

Google’s latest mid-sized sedan AI model is taking the world by storm. Gemini 4 Neon is technically the middle sibling in Google’s lineup, with Carbon at the top and Hydrogen at the bottom, but everyone seems to agree it absolutely cooks.

If you’ve spent any time on X over the past few days (I hate myself for writing that), you’ll likely have seen an uptick in fervor over Google’s latest model, which seems to outperform Claude Opus 5.5, and even Gemini 4 Carbon itself, in many benchmarks and real-world tests. Even Google is providing some helpful guidance about when to use one or the other.

One thing I’ve read again and again about Neon is how adept it is at writing. I’m of two minds about this: the better an AI gets at doing my job, the less necessary I am at said job. On the other hand, I’m so tired of obvious AI slop that a model that actually writes well sounds like a relief. At least when I’m unemployed, I won’t be yelling at the screen all day about why the robot yet again used negative parallelism.

I didn’t get to play much GTA VI over the weekend, but I know a few (million) people who did. Publisher Take-Two says the game generated $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales. That’s an incredible number in any industry, but a truly mind-blowing one in the video game world. Rockstar also released its first patch for the game on Monday to fix a modest number of bugs with the launch code.

If you follow open-weight AI models, you’ll likely have heard of how influential Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 was when it launched in June. Now the company has released GLM-5.4, and it’s novel as much for its architecture as it is for its benchmarks.

Its Loop Transformer reuses a block of layers to do more computation without adding parameters. The company is pitching applications beyond software, including games, visual work, and CAD. The 750-million-parameter model reportedly performs at the level of a 2-3 trillion parameter non-looping equivalent, but we’re still waiting on a broader release for real-world testing.

In browser news, Ladybird’s first public alpha is now downloadable for macOS and Linux. It’s built with a brand-new engine that eschews many of the legacy decisions made by Google’s Chromium team. And the project has the backing of big names like Shopify, Cloudflare, and Proton. It’s still pretty rough, and features are paltry, but any new competition in the browser space is a win in my book.

title: Anthropic just gave Claude users a new way to make Mac apps
snippet: Use Claude on Mac or Windows? Anthropic just released a new way to make personalized desktop apps using AI tools. more…
fullText:
Use Claude on Mac or Windows? Anthropic just released a new way to make personalized desktop apps using AI tools. 

Claude now lets you turn custom tools into personal desktop apps for Mac and Windows

“Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The “Install as app” feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows,” Anthropic says.

“When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow.”

Additionally, Anthropic says apps made with this method can benefit from Claude connectors. Claude usage is tied to desktop apps made with artifacts. 

This form of Claude-created app is capable of sending notifications, adding items to the menu bar, and having its own permissions.

title: Android app developers will have to publicly post address, phone number in 2027
snippet: Following new regulations, Google Play will require Android app developers to publicly post a business address starting in 2027 and, while there are workarounds, it’s not going to be the easiest thing. more…
fullText:
Following new regulations, Google Play will require Android app developers to publicly post a business address starting in 2027 and, while there are workarounds, it’s not going to be the easiest thing.

New Digital Services Act regulations in the EU and UK will require developers to share a phone number and address publicly. While this is only required in those regions, this information will be visible worldwide. Google does not allow PO boxes to be used for this requirement, meaning that many smaller developers will be left with limited options beyond posting their own personal address.

Exceptions to the rule include apps that are not published in the UK or Europe, or developers that qualify as “non-traders” which is essentially those making no money off of their apps.

Here’s how Google defines a “trader” in the context of Android apps:

	

Profit-seeking motive: you receive or intend to receive remuneration for your apps (for example, paid apps, in-app purchases, ad-sponsored apps) on a regular or commercial basis.

Transaction volume: you have a high or consistent number, amount, or frequency of transactions.

Business setup: you manage your app development and publishing as a business.

Legal status: you have a legal status (such as a D-U-N-S number) that enables you to engage in commercial activities

The Verge notes that a “registered agent service” can be used as a business address for those who don’t have a physical office, and that Apple is allowing iOS developers to use a PO box if they prove the box is linked to a physical address.

Google will require Android app developers to confirm their trader status and their address by February 1, 2027. Account-wide status can be found in the Google Play Console via Manage account > Account details > About you, while status on a per-app basis can be handled via Monitor and improve > Policy and programs > App content.
