The Keychron G6 HE, as its name indicates, also uses Hall effect switches for that same kind of customization. But something felt immediately off as I began testing it. The mouse's shape and design are very reminiscent of Logitech G Pro models, with more colorful flair. The magnetic switches are there and easily … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
When Keychron announced its $90 G6 HE gaming mouse, I immediately thought, “Cool! A cheaper alternative to the pricey $180 Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike.” Logitech’s innovation with the Superstrike is using magnetic Hall effect switches for a user-adjustable mouse click depth, with haptic vibrations mimicking the tactile click feel. The Keychron G6 HE, as its name indicates, also uses Hall effect switches for that same kind of customization. But something felt immediately off as I began testing it.

The mouse’s shape and design are very reminiscent of Logitech G Pro models, with more colorful flair. The magnetic switches are there and easily customizable (through a browser-based app, no less). But the clicks? The clicks are all wrong.

The left and right mouse buttons on the G6 HE use Keychron’s MagOptic switches, which are both magnetic Hall effect and optical. They click just like any standard mouse, regardless of where you set the actuation point. There are no fancy haptics on the Keychron. If you set the buttons to a shallow hair-trigger depth, you’ll register a press before you actually feel or hear any click. Set the depth for a very heavy press, and the mouse clicks before it actually registers. That… kind of defeats the purpose here.

$75

There’s not much point in tuning the actuation depth of the G6 HE’s buttons if the click feel doesn’t match it. I suppose it’s still nice to have a hair-trigger-like setting for taking faster single shots in an FPS, but not feeling anything when you shoot is weird. And it gets frustrating when using the G6 HE as a regular mouse for productivity — like you’re getting phantom clicks as you mouse around your computer. At least I can feel my accidental clicks when using a Logitech Superstrike with the action set too high, and I know I’m to blame for leaving the mouse on my try-hard settings.

I reached out to Keychron for the reasoning behind the G6 HE’s magnetic-but-not-haptic setup, and cofounder Fab Chan said, “There are two reasons for this design. First, many users still prefer the feel of a traditional click over haptics. Second, a haptic motor adds weight, and for this model we prioritized a lighter design. That said, we’re planning a model with haptic feedback. It will be slightly heavier than the G6 HE, and we’ll share more details soon.”

1/8Frosted lavender is a sharp look. It also comes in frosted black, pink, and mint colors.

The G6 HE is a lightweight mouse. It’s only 49g with its battery, or 40g in wired mode with the battery removed. The Logitech X2 Superstrike is 60g, and the newer X3 Superstrike is 59g — each still pretty light. If you ignore all the Hall effect stuff and just use the G6 HE as a regular mouse, it has some things going for it over the Superstrikes. In addition to its lighter build and much lower price, it feels a tiny bit comfier in my hand, thanks to its side walls that curve slightly inward at the bottom.

One of its best features is hot-swappable batteries. From my time testing Angry Miao’s AM Infinity Mouse, I know that once you can pop out a magnetic battery pack and quickly swap it, you never want to go back to plugging in your mouse to charge. You can also get the G6 HE in black with a standard built-in rechargeable battery for $15 less, but I don’t think that’s enough savings to forgo the convenience of hot-swap batteries.

The G6 HE’s charging base doubles as the wireless receiver, and of course it’s lit up with customizable RGB lighting. It has four programmable buttons for on-the-fly changes to things like DPI, lighting, mouse profiles, or just about anything else you want to program. The browser-based Keychron Launcher software is robust and makes tinkering with the G6 HE or its base very easy. And for some reason, the receiver / charging base is designed like a vacuum tube, which is fun, but it means you’re unscrewing its clear housing to access the battery — a little tedious.

Keychron’s Launcher web app is very simple to use. It works much like VIA for keyboards, but it’s tailored to Keychron boards and mice.

I can’t shake my disappointment with the G6 HE’s lackadaisical magnetic switch implementation. Keychron seems proud of the fancy MagOptic Switch it put into the G6 HE, even going so far as to call it “next gen,” but this mouse seems a jack of all trades and master of none. The G6 HE is cheaper than most other mice with hot-swap batteries — which can still make it worthwhile if you don’t care about all the Hall effect stuff — but that is its lone saving grace.

We’ll have to wait and see if Keychron’s follow-up model with haptics can properly compete with the Superstrike mice and their hallmark feature. I’m excited to see where Hall effect tech goes in mice, and how more companies can evolve it, but the G6 HE is a half-measure.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

The report cites “multiple sources” and comes from MacRumors. There aren’t any specific details about what changes iOS 28 will introduce for notifications. “The sources said iOS 28 will include significant changes to Notification Center, but we do not have any specific details,” the report says.

The iOS notifications system is overdue for an update. While Apple has added features like Apple Intelligence-based priority notifications and notification summaries, the system still lacks other organization and sorting settings.

Android 16 introduced several significant notification changes, focused primarily on reducing clutter and prioritizing important information. For Pixel devices, the update also introduced Notification Organizer, a feature that automatically groups and silences low-priority alerts, including promotions, news, and social media notifications.

As Abner explained on 9to5Google last year:

The Notification Organizer will sort your alerts into the following categories: Promotions, News, Social, and Suggested. The first two are already on, but you must enable the remaining ones. There’s also an option to “Always expand bundles.”

I’d love for Apple to adopt a similar system on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Even with the recent Apple Intelligence additions, the iOS notifications system is still far too basic.

title: Lenovo Legion Go Beam leaks with Android instead of SteamOS
snippet: The variety of gaming handhelds from Lenovo is about to get larger. Leaked details suggest the Lenovo Legion Go Beam will run Android instead of SteamOS on a high-refresh display. more…
fullText:
The variety of gaming handhelds from Lenovo is about to get larger. Leaked details suggest the Lenovo Legion Go Beam will run Android instead of SteamOS on a high-refresh display.

Lenovo is sticking with the Legion Go branding to offer something a little different to users. Instead of a SteamOS or Windows device, the Legion Go Beam is said to run Android (via Windows Latest). Specifically, Android 16.

That doesn’t limit it to Android titles alone. Android happens to make the perfect platform for cloud game streaming. Services like GeForce Now, Xbox Game Pass, and more offer a comparable experience to what a PC does for a fixed subscription, and that’s without the hardware internals something like the Legion Go 2 would need to run games natively.

The leak also notes the Lenovo Legion Go Beam will have a 7-inch 120Hz display, though there’s no information on what resolution or panel type the handheld might have. It’s likely 1080p or higher, though a lower resolution obviously will net users better performance. Battery is up in the air, too, other than a standard “long-lasting battery life” claim attributed to Lenovo.

	

This handheld takes a lot from the Legion Go 2 in design, as it should. It’s a comfortable device, and this shouldn’t be any different. It lacks a trackpad in favor of a traditional controller layout. It also has standard ports like one USB-C and 3.5mm headphone jack.

Pricing is a mystery. Devices like the Logitech G Cloud were such a hit because they delivered the needed performance at a good price. But those handhelds had a lower refresh rate. Still, hoping for a price tag around $350 or less isn’t such a bad thing.

title: Things 3.25 update brings new touch features to the MacBook Pro
snippet: Cultured Code is bringing swipe gestures to Things on Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro. Version 3.25 builds on the task manager’s basic touch support so you can schedule a to-do with a swipe or select several tasks with two fingers and drag them all at once. more…
fullText:
Cultured Code is bringing swipe gestures to Things on Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro. Version 3.25 builds on the task manager’s basic touch support so you can schedule a to-do with a swipe or select several tasks with two fingers and drag them all at once.

Swipe to schedule, select, and move to-dos

Say you’re going through your Today list and want to put something off until tomorrow. Swipe right on the to-do to open the date picker. Open it by touch and you’ll see taller rows that make dates easier to tap. Custom menus get the same treatment.

Swiping left selects a to-do. Swipe left again to deselect it. For a longer list, swipe up or down with two fingers to select several items at once. Then touch and hold any selected item to pick up the whole group, even if some of those tasks are offscreen. You can also drag individual to-dos and headings.

A single tap selects a to-do, and a second tap expands it. Double-tapping works too. Inside a to-do, checklist items are easier to reorder by touch. You can also cancel a to-do or checklist item by pressing and holding its checkbox.

Cultured Code has also made the sidebar easier to resize with a finger and given buttons throughout the Mac app larger tap targets.

The update follows Siri AI and Spotlight integration in Things 3.24 and more flexible scheduling for repeating to-dos in Things 3.23. You can find Things for Mac on the Mac App Store.

title: The Moto G Stylus (2025) at $200 is great only if a pen is a must
snippet: Okay, so here’s the deal (literally): last year’s Moto G Stylus (2025) is on sale right now on Amazon for just $199, and if you desperately need a digital writing tool with your phone, it’s a good buy. more…
fullText:
Okay, so here’s the deal (literally): last year’s Moto G Stylus (2025) is on sale right now on Amazon for just $199, and if you desperately need a digital writing tool with your phone, it’s a good buy.

That is the short answer; the long answer is a little more complicated, as due to some issues with the 2026 model, you are missing out on exactly…nothing. Yes, at under $200, you are getting essentially the same phone because Motorola decided that, due to RAM and storage shortages and price hikes, the newer model would forgo any major upgrades. The 2026 model starts at $499, so if you had your eye on it, yeah, it’s a silly way to waste $300 in our opinion.

It has the same Snapdragon 6 Gen 3 processor, 8GB RAM, and 128GB storage. There’s a 120Hz display too and the good news is you get a microSD card slot to expand the storage if you desperately need it. Other notable features include a 5,000mAh battery, 68W wired charging, 15W wireless charging, a 50MP camera setup, and, as of writing, it should be due for an Android 16 upgrade.

The star of the show of the Moto G Stylus (2025) is the stylus. It boils down to this: if you want a phone that isn’t a Galaxy Ultra, then this is the only other line that makes sense for document signers.

	

However, there are better deals out there. I think the Galaxy A56, at just $299, is an incredible offer right now and way more deserving of your hard-earned cash. Even so, if you want clean software or that stylus, the Moto G Stylus (2025) at $199 is at least an option especially for a family member or a backup to your existing phone.

title: CAD images suggest iPhone 18e will have an odd new camera design
snippet: CAD images of the iPhone 18e, said to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump. If accurate, it would represent a big change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau … more…
fullText:
CAD images of the iPhone 18e, said to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a big change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau …

The iPhone 17e was launched in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same. 

The current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but says that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito says he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

title: iOS 27.3 release date: Here’s when new iPhone features are coming
snippet: iOS 27.3 is coming soon, packed with new features for iPhone users. Here’s when to expect the next big iPhone software update. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.3 is coming soon, packed with new features for iPhone users. Here’s when to expect the next big iPhone software update.

iOS 27.3 confirmed to launch in December, likely by mid-month

If you follow Apple closely, the company’s software release patterns quickly become clear.

For example, iOS 27.2 launched late last month around the same time as releases in years past. The only difference is that normally iOS 27.1 would launch in late October rather than 27.2. But since Apple made iOS 27.1 exclusive to iPhone Duo, all software releases for the iOS 27 cycle will be off by one number—despite following the same timing as ever.

That means iOS 27.3 is up next, and its release should align with historic patterns for x.2 updates.

Apple has confirmed that iOS 27.3 will launch to all users in December once beta testing concludes.

To get more precise though, here’s a sampling of release patterns for comparable x.2 updates the last few years:

iOS 26.2: Friday, December 12

iOS 18.2: Wednesday, December 11

iOS 17.2: Monday, December 11

Based on this pattern, iOS 27.3 is expected to release by mid-December.

Apple always tries to ship its last software update of the year with a little buffer before taking a holiday break. That way if any major issues arise, the company can develop a quick fix and push it out before much of the company takes time off.

Expect to see iOS 27.3 launch as early as the week of December 7, or on Monday, December 14 at the latest.

New features coming in iOS 27.3

iOS 27.3 is packed with lots of new features for iPhone users spanning various popular apps.

Here are some of the new features in iOS 27.3:

Apple TV: Video podcasts and vertical ‘Clips’ videos

Health: All-new redesigned app with many new features

Safari: Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more

Apple Music: Selfie Sing feature and updated lyrics view

Siri AI: New in-app actions, languages, and more

Calendar: Design updates for one-handed use

Fitness: Gym Strength program for Fitness+

iCloud+: Expanded AI usage limits and Shortcuts feature

iPhone Duo also benefits from three exciting new features, including face unlock, Reachability, and a new setting to automatically lock the device when closed.

Finally, iOS 27.3 brings the first Apple Intelligence features to China—though Siri AI is still missing.

title: YouTube appears to be quietly testing a new mute button in its video UI
snippet: Users are seeing the option to mute a video appear in the YouTube app on Android, but it isn’t showing up for everyone. more…
fullText:
Users are seeing the option to mute a video appear in the YouTube app on Android, but it isn’t showing up for everyone.

Screenshots of a new video control button have started appearing on Reddit over the last week. The posts haven’t exactly begun hot debates, but it’s an interesting UI change. A mute button now sits next to the fullscreen option in the left section of the video player. Tapping it does nothing other than cut audio, until it’s tapped again to unmute.

One user details the app version on their Pixel 11 Pro XL – version 21.46.522. They also note that other devices they’ve checked on the YouTube app versions don’t appear to show any sort of mute button in the UI. Without many comments on either post, it’s hard to nail down just how wide this rollout might be.

In reality, this seems like a very small UI design test for the YouTube app. YouTube will often select a small number of users to push experimental features to while they polish them further before release. Unlike features that Premium users get to test, these are locked.

	

It’s not necessarily a big change, but it’s sort of a confusing one. One wonders why a mute button is necessary. It also adds another button to accidentally hit when trying to tap the fullscreen option.

What do you think? If you’re seeing a mute button in the YouTube app, let us know your thoughts and what kind of phone you’re using.

title: WhatsApp testing stickers with audio, including make-your-own option
snippet: WhatsApp is currently testing a new sticker format that plays a sound when the recipient taps on it. You can choose from a range of standard stickers as well as create your own by converting a video … more…
fullText:
WhatsApp is currently testing a new sticker format that plays a sound when the recipient taps on it. You can choose from a range of standard stickers as well as create your own by converting a video … 

The feature was spotted by WABetaInfo in the beta version of the Android app. 

WhatsApp is developing a new format to add an audio track to a sticker. This would allow users to send a sticker that plays a sound when the recipient taps it. 

You can create your own audio stickers by selecting one of your videos.

Once users choose a video from their gallery, WhatsApp converts it into an animated sticker automatically. At the top of the editor, users can find a new audio button that lets them add a sound to the sticker. If users tap this button, WhatsApp will display a new “Add sound” screen. This section lets users refine the new sound sticker by choosing which audio track to attach to it.

Sounds don’t play automatically, but recipients will see a small audio icon attached to the sticker, and tapping it will play the sound.

As usual with WhatsApp, it’s rolling out first in the Android beta and is likely to reach the iPhone sometime later. This can range from a few weeks to a few months, depending on how well the beta test goes.

Who should buy the Galaxy Tab S12+?

The Galaxy Tab S12+ is the sweet spot if you want a serious upgrade over a basic tablet without moving to Samsung’s biggest screen.

As we covered in our Galaxy Tab S12 launch story, it combines a 12.6-inch 120Hz AMOLED display with a MediaTek Dimensity 9500 processor, 12GB of RAM, and an included S Pen, with four months of complimentary Adobe Photoshop access and a six-month Notability trial, both of which support the stylus.

The Galaxy Tab S12+ also offers a 5G version, making it worth considering if you regularly work away from Wi-Fi.

The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra is made for creative professionals and families seeking premium entertainment. It moves naturally between focused creative work and immersive movie nights at home.

Its 14.6-inch AMOLED display gives photos, drawings, and multiple app windows more breathing room. Picture reviewing a document while keeping your handwritten notes visible, or drawing with reference images alongside your canvas.

The Ultra shares the S12+’s Dimensity 9500 processor but offers configurations up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. It’s available for $1,399.99, but last year’s Tab S11 Ultra is on sale during Black Friday for just $899.99.

Both S12 tablets ship with Android 17-based One UI 9 and seven years of OS and security updates. Photoshop comes pre-installed with a four-month access offer, giving you a way to explore S Pen-assisted photo editing.

The Ultra is especially appealing with a keyboard at a desk; Samsung’s Ultra Book Cover Keyboard Slim is the perfect companion to the S12 Ultra, and is on sale for $146.99 during Best Buy’s Black Friday Deal event.

Is the Galaxy Tab S11 still a good buy?

Yes, the Galaxy Tab S11 is the premium Galaxy tablet to choose when portability comes first.

Our Galaxy Tab S11 launch coverage highlighted the return of Samsung’s smaller flagship tablet, with a Dimensity 9400+ processor, 12GB of RAM, and an included S Pen. Its 11-inch AMOLED screen makes it an attractive companion for reading, travel, and handwritten notes.

The Galaxy Tab S11 is the sort of tablet you can bring to a meeting or pull out on a train without needing a large work surface. You still get premium display quality, just in a size that’s easier to carry, and it comes in at a lower price.

A discounted Tab S11 Ultra can also be worth considering if you want a 14.6-inch screen. Compare the actual price with the S12 Ultra rather than dismissing an older flagship automatically.

Which Galaxy Tab offers the best everyday value?

The Galaxy Tab S10 FE and FE+ are compelling choices for people who want an included S Pen without flagship pricing.

Choose the 10.9-inch FE for a study companion that travels easily. Choose the 13.1-inch FE+ when you’d rather put a lecture, document, or recipe beside your notes. Both offer IP68 water and dust resistance, so they’re great kitchen companions.

Galaxy Tab S10 Lite is for students, children, and emerging creators. It is a practical, encouraging gift for handwritten learning, organization, drawing, and experimentation.

The Galaxy Tab A11+ is the straightforward entertainment choice. At $199, it’s the cheapest of the Galaxy Tab options, but it doesn’t support the S Pen, so choose an S-series model if handwriting matters.

Which Galaxy Tab is right for you?

Choose the Galaxy Tab S12+ for a premium all-rounder, the S12 Ultra for a spacious creative workspace, or the S11 for flagship features in a travel-friendly size.

For school, home projects, and everyday notes, the FE series delivers the features many people actually need. For family streaming and browsing, the A11+ keeps things simple and affordable.

The best Galaxy Tab isn’t automatically the biggest or newest. It’s the one that makes the things you already love doing easier — and gives you a few new possibilities along the way.

title: Google Maps update on Android Auto adds navigation routes for motorcycles
snippet: Google Maps is rolling out an update on Android Auto that provides better navigation routes specifically for motorcycles. more…
fullText:
Google Maps is rolling out an update on Android Auto that provides better navigation routes specifically for motorcycles.

Users in India have recently noticed that Google Maps for Android Auto is showing a new message asking them to restart the app to “switch to two-wheeler directions.” Once enabled, a motorcycle icon appears on the ETA card.

On a support page, Google details this mode, explaining that the mode tailors directions to skip routes where two-wheelers are not allowed, while also included narrow roads that may be faster. Google says that the feature is only available in “limited locations.”

These directions show you routes away from roads where two-wheelers aren’t allowed. You may be directed towards shortcuts along narrower side roads.

The page also explains that it is only available for mobile devices, with no mention of Android Auto and CarPlay. Yet, a number of users are seeing the adjustment on their devices within the past two weeks, so it seems Google is expanding it out to Android Auto. That makes sense, as Android Auto has been working to better accommodate motorcycles for a while, and some motorcycles even now have Android Auto support built-in.

title: I love YouTube on TV, but we desperately need better watchlist controls
snippet: Managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life. Google’s premier streaming app has too many issues with resurfacing content; in my opinion, this is now a major problem that needs to be fixed. more…
fullText:
Managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life. Google’s premier streaming app has too many issues with resurfacing content; in my opinion, this is now a major problem that needs to be fixed.

Aside from my YouTube watchlist gripes, it’s no secret that moving from a web browser to the TV is ultimately still a frustrating experience.

Lots of things I love about watching videos on my laptop or PC just don’t translate well to when I’m sat on my sofa holding a remote trying to find something to watch after wrapping up for the day. One thing I’m getting annoyed with is how YouTube scales on TV and Android TV boxes because you’re given less choice and arguably poorer recommendations for content due to the constraints in place.

Understandably, you can’t compress the layout too much on a TV as you’re typically sat a few feet away and all aspects of the interface need to be legible. I would still like to tweak it, though, if that were possible.

	

Maybe we could get proper sections for content, like how Netflix and other streaming platforms offer categorized areas where you can search for “comedy” or “horror”. I’m almost certain that, with Google’s insane investment and massive AI push, where every video is already analyzed hundreds of times, that wouldn’t be too difficult to do.

The problem now is that the sidebar menu is just too broad. Gaming covers basically everything. Then each line of videos accounts for one title, but requires search and previous watch data to populate. I find myself often fighting with recommendations on my TV, whereas on desktop it’s not as much of a problem.

That leads me to my biggest problem with YouTube, and it’s the, frankly, embarrassing watchlist or “Watch later” controls.

I can’t fault that it works, but right now the watchlist function is like something out of the early 2000s due to the lack of flexibility that I touched on above. As my YouTube consumption has increased 20x over the past four or five years, managing what I want to come back to or might have missed the first time around is starting to become a bit of a chore.

I’ve tried using playlists to save things, but things get messy very quickly because of how cumbersome it is to a) create a playlist on TV and b) how playlists are organized by default.

Google TV isn’t perfect, but it’s where I keep my biggest TV and movie watchlist outside of YouTube. Yes, YouTube is mostly for user-generated content, but I would take something as basic as Google TV’s interface baked into YouTube somehow. Add in categorization and auto-clear.

The Watch Later section has become an unwieldy place that I never really want to go unless I desperately have to. I’m constantly losing videos that I hoped to come back to or have an affinity for.

Videos don’t clear automatically, nor do you know when they were added. Yes, I’ll give credit that you can sort by a few options, but that’s the bare minimum. The process of moving things around is slow and takes multiple taps. Watch Later is also hidden compared to other services. It’s under your account, then beneath “Liked videos,” which is below any you may have uploaded yourself.

On a TV, the process is so annoying I just avoid it altogether. You go to the sidebar menu > Library > Watch later. It should be front-and-center on a TV. It’s almost unforgivable in my eyes because even your watch history is given greater prominence. I simply cannot understand that decision.

I’m not always a huge fan of AI being shoehorned into apps and services, but this is one of those areas that has been left to rot for a while and could get a big uplift from adding in a little bit of Gemini. Even if it were just an enhanced search function or more tools for organizing.

With YouTube TV effectively taking over regular broadcast television and being the world’s biggest streaming platform, I’m shocked by how so many areas of the platform remain in a consistently neglected state.

A little bit of spit and polish, and maybe I’ll start using this section again. For now, though, I’ll stick to texting myself links of stuff I want to watch. The ball is in your court, Google.

title: Which Samsung folding phone is right for you? Galaxy Z Fold 8, Ultra, or Flip 8
snippet: Folding phones are entering a new chapter and, if you’re looking to try one for the first time, you might not know exactly where to start. In this guide, we’ll take a look at some of the most important questions to answer when buying a foldable, and dissect how Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Galaxy Z Flip 8 fit the bill to figure out which is the best for you, especially if you’re interested in one this holiday season. more…
fullText:
Folding phones are entering a new chapter and, if you’re looking to try one for the first time, you might not know exactly where to start. In this guide, we’ll take a look at some of the most important questions to answer when buying a foldable, and dissect how Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Galaxy Z Flip 8 fit the bill to figure out which is the best for you, especially if you’re interested in one this holiday season.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 vs Fold 8 Ultra vs Flip 8: What you need to know

Samsung has three foldables in its lineup this year, two of which are pretty familiar. The Galaxy Z Flip 8 continues the lineup of clamshell-style foldables, offering a form factor similar to that of a classic flip phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, meanwhile, is designed to be a normal smartphone on the outside, hiding a tablet within. Finally, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the new kid on the block, offering a compact outer display that opens up to a media-friendly, wider inner panel.

Each one serves a different need, but they all share similar performance and core specs. Here’s a quick rundown of the key details on each device:

	

Galaxy Z Fold 8

Displays: 5.5-inch outer, 7.6-inch inner, both up to 120Hz

Thickness: 9.7mm when folded

Weight: 201 grams

Chip: Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy

Storage/RAM: Up to 1TB/16GB

Cameras: 50MP main, 50MP ultrawide, 10MP selfie (one on each display)

OS: One UI 9 based on Android 17

Battery: 4,800 mAh

Charging: 45W wired, 20W wireless

Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra

Displays: 6.5-inch outer, 8-inch inner, both up to 120Hz

Thickness: 8.9mm when folded

Weight: 215 grams

Chip: Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy

Storage/RAM: Up to 1TB/16GB

Cameras: 200MP main, 50MP ultrawide, 10MP 3x telephoto, 10MP selfie (one on each display)

OS: One UI 9 based on Android 17

Battery: 5,000 mAh

Charging: 45W wired, 20W wireless

Galaxy Z Flip 8

Displays: 4.1-inch outer, 6.9-inch inner, both up to 120Hz

Thickness: 13.1mm when folded

Weight: 180 grams

Chip: Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy

Storage/RAM: Up to 512GB/12GB

Cameras: 50MP main, 12MP ultrawide, 10MP selfie (on inner display)

OS: One UI 9 based on Android 17

Battery: 4,300 mAh

Charging: 25W wired, 15W wireless

Starting with the displays, the book-style Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra both provide outer displays that are fully usable as standard smartphones, while the inner display is useful for multitasking, media, or just getting more space for reading a website or e-book. Samsung’s top-tier specs deliver performance for everything you’d need, with Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy powering everything from demanding games or media-editing apps to day-to-day use.

With each Samsung foldable, you’re getting a fully capable smartphone, but finding the one that’s best for you is a matter of picking your most important priorities. Cameras, battery life, content consumption, and size are some of the most important points to consider, so let’s take a look one-by-one.

What Samsung foldable has the best cameras?

When it comes to cameras, foldables have a tough time. There’s only so much physical space to fit the camera sensors and, with cameras, having more space generally results in a battery overall camera.

That said, the best camera on a Samsung foldable is undoubtedly on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. 

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra has a 200MP main camera that’s similar to the Galaxy S26 Ultra, while it also packs a 50MP ultrawide and something neither of the others offer, a telephoto lens. The 10MP telephoto shooter captures faraway subjects at 3x optical zoom, meaning you’re not giving up on quality when you zoom in. Two 10MP cameras can be found on the displays, with neither sacrificing quality for an under-display look.

Runner-up here is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which offers a pair of 50MP cameras for wide and ultrawide shots. You can get 2x optical-quality zoom out of the main sensor to still get a good zoom shot, while the main camera still offers good quality and Samsung’s best camera features including 2x optical-quality zoom and the subject-tracking My FanCam.

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 may not have the best camera hardware, but what it lacks in hardware it makes up for in flexibility. This is definitely the best form factor of the bunch for using the foldable design as a tripod for capturing clips. All three devices also use their foldable nature to let you capture full-quality selfies using the rear cameras, which always have better quality than the 10MP dedicated front-facing cameras. 

What Samsung foldable has the best battery life?

Here’s where specs on paper can tell a different story compared to real life. 

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra may offer the biggest battery of the bunch at 5,000 mAh, but its battery life is on par with the smaller Galaxy Z Fold 8. Both foldables are designed to last you through a full day, though sticking to the outer display only on the Fold 8 Ultra may bring you slightly better battery life overall.

In either case, you’re also getting 45W fast charging over USB-C, granting you speedy recharging if your device happens to get low through the course of a busy day. These are also “Qi2 Ready,” meaning you can use magnetic wireless chargers if you use a compatible magnetic case.

Why buy a folding phone in the first place?

One of the most important things you’ll want to ask yourself when buying a foldable phone is why you want to opt for a foldable in the first place, and each of these devices gives a different answer.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is a productivity powerhouse, delivering more space on its inner display for you to get work done through the web, apps, and more. You can run up to three apps at once on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s display, as well as floating apps, and more. 

Galaxy Z Fold 8 is great for media consumption. The wider aspect ratio is perfect for watching videos, playing games, reading books, and more, all while still giving you plenty of space for productivity just like the Ultra. 

Galaxy Z Flip 8, meanwhile, is all about giving you a more compact device. The outer display lets you quickly reply to messages or keep up with directions, while you can unfold it to do everything you want to on a normal phone. Close it up to more easily stow it away in your pocket or your bag.

Can I transfer everything from my old phone?

If you are moving into a new Galaxy foldable, the good news is that you don’t have to start from scratch. Thanks to Samsung’s Smart Switch app, you can easily transfer supported content including pictures, contacts, messages, and more from an older Galaxy phone, another Android phone, or even an iPhone over to a Galaxy foldable. Apps, messages, photos, and more can all make the move wirelessly, without the need of a cable.

Where to buy a Samsung foldable

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the best places to score a great deal with solid trade-in values and deep discounts around Black Friday and throughout the holiday season.

title: AirTag 2 has two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade
snippet: AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade. more…
fullText:
AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

#1: Precision Finding works from much greater distances

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

This expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

#2: Significantly louder built-in speaker

When you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company says this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the new speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that users are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

title: Google Maps might change its colors again, but it’s optional this time [Gallery]
snippet: Google Maps has a pretty consistent style, but a new option appears to be in the works with a darker “high-visibility” setting. more…
fullText:
Google Maps has a pretty consistent style, but a new option appears to be in the works with a darker “high-visibility” setting.

The last major change to Google Maps styling came in 2023 (yes, time flies) when the platform rolled out a new color palette to all users. This was divisive among users, but ultimately worked out. 

Now, Google appears to be working on another new shake-up.

The folks over at Android Authority spotted a new “high-visibility” toggle in the latest Google Maps update for Android, with the new style having darker colors for the map in both light and dark modes, as well as a purple line for your route compared to the blue we’re used to seeing. 

	

Standard
High-visibility
Standard
High-visibility

The change was also spotted on Android Auto, with much darker colors (including a near-black dark mode) in both color settings for your car’s display. This is likely tied to this new “High-visibility” setting, but it’s hard to say for certain – teardowns and enabling new features early can only tell us so much.

This appears to all be controlled by a new “Map style” setting in Google Maps, with “Standard” and “High-visibility” settings available. Functionally, everything remains the same, it’s just a new set of colors. 

So, where the previous color changes were forced on all users, this one is at least optional, and the “High-visibility” naming seems like it’s targeted at those with difficulties in sight more so than just a general change for all users.

fullText:
The Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is worth spending more on if you want longer battery life, a brighter outdoor display, and specialized features for trail running and diving. The Galaxy Watch 9 is the better fit if you want Samsung’s latest everyday health tools in a smaller, lighter watch.

Both, however, are fantastic smartwatches with limitless potential. They share a Snapdragon Wear Elite processor and many of Samsung’s newest wellness features, so deciding between them is really about figuring out your priorities when it comes to buying a wearable this holiday season. We’re here to help you figure that out.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

What do the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 and Watch 9 have in common?

As we covered in our Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 comparison, both watches move to Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform. Both also ship with Wear OS 7 and One UI 8 Watch.

	

That shared foundation includes useful health insights. Vitals brings overnight measurements together to establish your personal baseline, while Daily Cardio Load helps you understand training demands and recovery. Hearing monitoring can flag potentially unsafe noise levels, whether you’re at a concert or somewhere unexpectedly loud.

Both also get five years of Wear OS updates and security patches, making either a useful long-term partner for your Samsung device, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra or Galaxy Z Fold8.

How do their specifications compare?

The clearest differences are size, battery capacity, display brightness, and outdoor capabilities. Here’s how the lineup breaks down:

As you can tell, the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is considerably bigger and heavier, but you get a lot more capability for that additional size. 

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 makes its strongest case when your plans regularly take you beyond a desk, a gym, or a charger.

Samsung rates the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for up to 60 hours with the always-on display enabled, compared with up to 30 hours for the Watch 9, and that extra headroom is appealing when your day starts with a workout and finishes well into the evening.

Then there’s the screen. In our hands-on with both watches, the Ultra 2’s brightness stood out immediately, with a higher peak that gives it an advantage when checking workout information outdoors, even in the bright sun. And its titanium frame provides added durability.

The Ultra 2 also adds Trail Run tracking for elevation and terrain impact, route guidance using compatible GPX files, and Nutrition Alert hydration guidance. These are tangible reasons to upgrade if your usual run involves trails instead of pavement.

Diving is another differentiator. Samsung specifies recreational diving support to depths of up to 40 meters, with automatic tracking of depth, dive time and water temperature — a remarkable feat for a piece of technology that lives on your wrist.

How would you use these watches in everyday life?

The best choice becomes clearer when you picture your own routine:

A busy workweek: The Watch 9 handles everyday activity and sleep tracking without the Ultra’s larger footprint. Its lighter case is especially appealing if you want to wear your watch through meetings, workouts, and bedtime.

A weekend on the trails: The Ultra 2 lets you follow a prepared route and check elevation as the climb gets steeper. Its brighter display makes a quick glance more useful when you’d rather keep moving than shade the screen.

Training for a race: Both offer Daily Cardio Load, so recovery guidance isn’t reserved for the expensive model. Choose the Ultra 2 when trail-specific tools and extra battery headroom also fit your training.

A trip with full days out: The Ultra 2’s longer rated endurance offers more flexibility between charges. The Watch 9’s smaller design may be more appealing if you prioritize comfortable overnight wear and can charge during your daily routine.

Which Galaxy Watch should you buy?

Choose the Galaxy Watch 9 for everyday wellness, a lighter fit, and strong value. Choose the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for longer adventures, more demanding outdoor activities, and greater freedom between charges.

If you’re replacing an older Galaxy Watch, both offer a compelling new generation of health insights and long-term support. Both last a long time and look absolutely awesome with running shorts or a business suit. But the Watch Ultra 2 can take you that extra mile, literally and figuratively, and may be worth spending more on during Best Buy’s Holiday Deals event.

title: YouTube’s iconic iOS app icon may soon return with new customizable icons [Gallery]
snippet: The iconic YouTube app icon that looked like a retro TV found on iOS might be making a comeback, with new customizable icons showing up behind the scenes of a new YouTube update. more…
fullText:
The iconic YouTube app icon that looked like a retro TV found on iOS might be making a comeback, with new customizable icons showing up behind the scenes of a new YouTube update.

In the early days of the iPhone, Apple built a custom app for YouTube on iOS before Google built its own. That included an app icon that looked like a retro TV and it was later replaced when YouTube’s official app launched on the platform. 

Now, that icon might be coming back.

Android Authority spotted several new app icons YouTube for Android is testing in its latest beta update (v21.47.483-BETA). These icons seem to be tied to a new feature that would allow users to customize the homescreen icon for YouTube, and includes seven designs in total including two throwback designs. One is the aforementioned retro TV icon used on iOS, which was never on YouTube for Android, and another is an old stacked YouTube logo design. 

	

Users would be able to change the app icon via a new setting in the app near the “Appearance” section, but nothing is live just yet. We also don’t know if this is Android-only, if this is limited to Premium subscribers, or when this might debut.

That said, it’s very fun to get these throwbacks, and we’ll be excited to see this functionality go live.

title: Apple Mail added four convenient new features in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 brought new features to Apple Wallet, Maps, Notes, Messages, and more—and it includes key upgrades for the Mail app too. Here’s everything new for Apple Mail in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 brought new features to Apple Wallet, Maps, Notes, Messages, and more—and it includes key upgrades for the Mail app too. Here’s everything new for Apple Mail in iOS 27.

Upgraded search

If you have much history using Apple Mail, you’ll know that its search feature hasn’t always been the best. But in iOS 27, search has gotten a big upgrade.

From Apple’s website:

More relevant search in Mail. A new ranking system brings the most relevant results to the top to help you find what you need right away — even if it’s buried deep in your inbox.

I can’t count the number of times search has previously failed to find messages that I knew existed. So far in my usage, iOS 27 has fixed that.

New suggestions that include third-party apps

Suggestions at the top of messages have been in Apple Mail for years. But in iOS 27, they have a new, more flexible design and expand to support third-party apps.

When Mail detects that you might want to take action on the contents of an email, a suggestion might appear at the top of the message. These include: directions in Maps, creating events in Calendar, tracking a shipment with Apple Wallet, and more.

In iOS 27, third-party apps can offer suggestions too. And when multiple apps are available with suggested actions, there’s a drop-down menu to show you all available options.

Smart Reply improvements

Smart Reply is a keyboard feature that automatically surfaces reply options you can utilize with a single tap.

In iOS 27, the next generation of Apple Intelligence comes with improvements to Smart Reply.

Apple says that Smart Reply “can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.” Essentially, rather than offering fairly generic reply options, now Smart Reply suggestions will actually sound a lot more like you.

Siri AI capabilities

Apple has added ‘Ask Siri’ buttons throughout Apple Mail, just like the rest of its system apps. And Siri AI brings a bunch of new powers for Mail users.

One example I’ve seen several times on social media is that you can ask Siri to delete all messages from a specific sender that’s spamming you.

Bug fixes

Beyond new features, Apple also says that iOS 27 makes the Mail app run better than ever thanks to bug fixes and performance improvements. Here are some specific examples given:

Faster message loading in Mail

More reliable search indexing in Mail

Improved list formatting in Mail

Improved unread badge accuracy in Mail

title: iPhone Duo Diary: Pros & cons in early real-life use
snippet: I said back at the launch that I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo despite feeling that it wasn’t the best match for me. A hands-on session of around half an hour in an Apple Store didn’t change either impression. But there’s of course no substitute for real-life usage of a device to find out how accurate my initial impressions might be, so I’m currently using the Duo as my sole iPhone, leaving my iPhone 18 Pro in a drawer … more…
fullText:
I said back at the launch that I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo despite feeling that it wasn’t the best match for me. A hands-on session of around half an hour in an Apple Store didn’t change either impression.

But there’s of course no substitute for real-life usage of a device to find out how accurate my initial impressions might be, so I’m currently using the Duo as my sole iPhone, leaving my iPhone 18 Pro in a drawer …

The launch video already had me wanting one, despite my view that it wasn’t really designed for me.

This device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo.

Using one in an Apple Store reinforced both sides of the equation for me.

Yes, it’s exceedingly expensive, and yes, having the priciest iPhone lack the best cameras would be a huge compromise for me. But while I still don’t think it would be the best iPhone for my needs, I do absolutely, undeniably want one.

What I’m doing now is using the iPhone Duo as my primary phone to discover how those pros and cons balance out in the real world. This first piece is written after just a couple of days, so compromises the things that stand out to me in very early use.

Pros

The large inner display

The size of the inner display is, of course, the whole point of the device: you essentially get an iPad mini that slips into your pocket. As someone who will almost always take a larger display over a smaller one, I do really love this.

When using a single app full screen on the display, it’s significantly more immersive than on other iPhones. For example, it’s normally extremely rare for me to ever watch video on an iPhone screen, but although I would still opt for a MacBook over the iPhone Duo, I have found myself watching more YouTube videos on the device. It does depend to an extent on the aspect ratio of the video, however, with letterboxing reducing the appeal.

It can be a much better way to casually share photos and iPhone videos with other people. I never feel that even a Pro Max screen does justice to most photos, but the iPhone Duo screen can be large enough to do so. This again, however, depends on the aspect ratio. For example, a photo in a 16:9 ratio or similar is actually smaller on this display than it is on a Pro Max.

But a photo with the same aspect ratio as the display, completely filling it, really does look great.

My preference for large screens extends to ebooks, so reading an ebook on an iPhone has always been an absolute last resort. However, while doing so on the Duo certainly wouldn’t be my first choice, it is a significantly better experience than a normal iPhone. I’m currently viewing it as part of my Kindle ecosystem: iPhone Duo, Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, Kindle Scribe.

Provided an app has been optimized for the display, pretty much everything is just better on this size screen

The anti-reflective coating

While the size may be the headline news, I have to say I’m also a huge fan of the anti-reflective coating. I said when I first tested it that I wished it had also been used on the outer display and was an option on other iPhones, and I’m absolutely still of this view.

It’s almost as if it turns it into a third display type, sitting somewhere between e-ink and conventional glossy screens. I know some find the colors too muted compared to a glossy display, but I don’t find this to be an issue at all. I very much prefer the more paper-like look.

Split view

Split-screen view, positioning one app on each side of the display, is another key feature. The display is too small for windowing, but the split-screen view is very usable for short tasks. It’s especially useful when using two apps simultaneously, such as embedding a photo into a message.

Another handy use is when you’re following instructions in one app to carry out in another – in this case Claude telling me how to transfer an e-SIM from my 18 Pro to the Duo (which it did better than Siri AI <sigh>).

The new gesture of sliding from the bottom of the screen to either the left or right side became instinctive almost immediately – it’s just so obvious. You can also quit either app while leaving the other in place.

Dual-camera view in FaceTime

I had a FaceTime call last night where I was able to let my friend see both my face and what I was looking at. Admittedly, I was mostly using this feature to show off the iPhone Duo itself in a mirror, but I can definitely see situations in which this would be genuinely useful, ranging from tech support to sharing travel experiences.

The outer display usability

The aspect ratio of the outer display definitely takes some getting used to, but you can display the same number of apps as on a standard iPhone. I also found that reachability in one-handed use was better with this than with the iPhone Pro Max, so I view this as a win for the device.

Pocketability

Finally, of course, the other side of the USP of the Duo is the small folded size. The shape is extremely pocketable and fits jeans pockets more comfortably than even a standard iPhone Pro, let alone the Pro Max. At the same time, the increased width is still narrow enough to comfortably fit into a standard jacket/coat inside pocket.

Cons

The camera compromises

I’ve talked about this a lot already as the biggest disincentive for me to buy the Duo, so I’ll just briefly reiterate the key differences here. No telephoto lens*, none of the new Pro controls like variable aperture and shutter speed, no ProRAW photos, no ProRes RAW video. 

*This one isn’t huge for me as I mostly shoot in the 0.5 to 2x range, but there are definitely times when longer reach is useful.

The weight

The Duo is heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and I have to say that you do feel the weight in one-handed use. While you’re using the outer display, the trade-off is very poor: you’re getting a heavier device with a smaller screen.

When using the inner display, it still feels heavy and isn’t comfortable to hold with one hand, in part due to the lever effect, so I generally hold it with both hands. That’s perfectly usable, with everything within reach of one thumb or the other, and of course the trade-off is very much more reasonable given the size of the display you’re now using.

In my own usage so far, I’ve opened up the phone for anything other than really quick things like checking an incoming message. But if you’re someone who would mostly use the outer screen, as was the case with my colleague Ryan, then I can see why the Duo simply wouldn’t make sense.

The bulk

Closely related to the weight when using the device in folded form, it feels rather bulky, especially with a case on it – and given the extremely high price of a replacement screen, you’d have to be very brave indeed to use it without one!

Touch ID

Perhaps I’ll get used to it, but in the first few days the lack of Face ID has annoyed me Every Single Time I’ve had to unlock the phone or use biometric authentication within an app. Face ID is just so seamless, and Touch ID very much isn’t.

The issue is exacerbated by the fact that the button will be in a different place depending on which way you’re holding the phone, and using it in different orientations is very much more common with the Duo than with a conventional slab iPhone.

The rest-to-unlock setting helps a little, but not much. I’m running it on the developer beta, so I do have Face Unlock enabled, but while I think Apple’s compromises make sense, the practical impact is that it demands Touch ID most of the time.

When I heard the level of complaints being made about the downgrade to Touch ID, I thought people were perhaps making too much fuss about the issue, but even three days in, I have to say I now get it completely.

Unoptimised apps

One of the early adopter pains is unoptimized apps. A lot of them will get fixed quite quickly, I think, but there are always apps that never will – like banking apps. However, this is a smaller issue than I expected it to be.

For example, my development has a concierge app used for things like notifying me when packages have been delivered to the front desk instead of my apartment. With the iPhone Duo unfolded in landscape mode, this app initially opened as a tiny vertical window. However, as soon as I hit the on-screen buttons to flip and resize an unoptimized app, then it became perfectly usable – and it has remembered this setting ever since.

The cost

The final drawback, and a very substantial one, is of course the cost. Yes, it combines the benefits of an iPhone and an iPad mini in one device, but it literally costs the same as buying each of them. Just a few years ago, if you had talked about anyone spending $2,000 plus on a iPhone, it would have seemed absolutely insane. I’m honestly not sure it’s any less insane today.

However, if you do want both devices and would otherwise have bought each of them, then there’s definitely a massive convenience factor in having it all in one pocketable package. 

Early conclusions

I said in the intro that there was a definite head versus heart thing going on here. Given the importance of the camera functionality, my head is quite certain that the iPhone 18 Pro is the better device for me. My heart, however, is finding the Duo a dangerously compelling proposition in all other respects.

My head also wanted to cheat. It proposed that I should carry both devices, using the 18 Pro as a camera and the Duo for everything else. It has taken considerable willpower to reject this idea and leave the 18 Pro at home; that in itself tells its own story.

Even in the first few days, some of the novelty factor has already worn off. For example, that clever blur animation as you unfold the phone is super-cute the first few times you see it, but now I no longer even notice it. The overall excitement of a brand new form factor will similarly wear off over time, though I’m not sure at what rate.

In previous head versus heart battles, I’ve certainly made mistakes in some areas of my life. In the tech sphere, however, my head usually wins out. Right now, then, I have two predictions. First, I’m not going to end up as an iPhone Duo owner. Second, I’m going to be exceedingly sad when I return it.

Place your bets …

title: Like clockwork, the Pixel 11 is a way better buy after a few months [Video]
snippet: Like clockwork, the first quarter of the Pixel 11 brings discounts, and this shines a light on the base model that needs to be explored. more…
fullText:
Like clockwork, the first quarter of the Pixel 11 brings discounts, and this shines a light on the base model that needs to be explored.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

By this point, you don’t need me to tell you that this is a familiar design. It’s turning into a comfortable pair of slippers at this point in time. Nothing is wrong, and nothing particularly stands out. A safe but samey design that is inoffensive.

	

I hoped that the maximum brightness bug would have been resolved by now with the screen. It creates a shadow around the edges of the display after a minute or so when in direct sunlight. Somewhat like blooming on a cheap LCD screen. It does diminish what is otherwise a great display.

The thickness has started to feel like a relic of the 2023 design that feels a little dated now. I have been using the Pixel 11 without a case most of the time, which mitigates it, but throw a case on and it’s a chunky boi. The added thickness would probably have been acceptable had the extra space been filled with more battery, but it feels like that boat has set sail a long time ago. A slimmer profile probably would have helped differentiate without deviating too much from last year’s phone.

After months of using the Pixel 11, the move of the NFC module to the top edge has been huge for me because my car uses an NFC terminal to lock and unlock when you’re without a set of car keys. With the Pixel 10, it worked but not quite as smoothly. It’s one of those inconsequential changes that makes a real-world difference.

Gemini Intelligence has been something I’ve started to rely on quite heavily. I love that I get a prompt to add an appointment to my calendar, and all of the important details have been taken care of, like the location, extra contact details, the works.

I’m not sure what the hold-up is for adding wider functionality. It’s actively hurting things, in my opinion. Google Messages is great, but some of the automation functions locked in there mean I haven’t been saving any time with Gemini’s prowess at doing the legwork of keeping my life up to date.

I’ve tried using Pause Point, but found it’s just easier to leave my phone face down rather than use an app to try and stop using my phone…maybe if we all did that, so many of the world’s ills wouldn’t be so pronounced. Just a thought.

The November Pixel Drop has also made some notable changes to the Pixel 11 experience that I can’t believe were held back since launch. If you waited and bought in the last few weeks with the substantial discounts kicking around, you objectively get a better phone today than at launch.

The improvements don’t overhaul things, just enhance or heighten the fluidity and experience above what was available in the months post-launch. More cohesive theming, little tweaks to the UI; it’s not reinventing the Pixel 11, just augmenting it in ways that would have been nice back in August.

I don’t really have much to complain about with the Pixel 11 lifespan even after months of charging. Yes, charging is still slow, but you only need to charge once per day. If we were talking about a phone with bad battery life and slow charging, I’d have more to complain about. However, it’s still solid and dependable.

Look, a “new” camera

The camera continues to impress without really improving drastically. I can’t help but feel that every couple of generations, the Pro camera setup should be passed on to the base Pixel, then we get a newer, improved system on that specific Pro model. It’d allow for quicker improvements and maybe, dare I say it, make the camera system cheaper as parts get reused. If anything, it would help Google’s supposed environmental pledges by preventing camera components from hitting landfill.

What I learned after 30 days with the Pixel 11 [Video]

A lot of people will tell you the best camera is the one you have with you, and this hasn’t ever been a problem for a recent Pixel. I can count on one hand the frustrations I have felt with the Pixel 11 camera since it landed on my desk on launch day. I am happier than a year ago with the base Pixel 10 than the 11, which is to say this is a bigger leap or a return to form.

Having the ability to tune Camera Looks was something I have loved, but you might just fall into using one tuned look that fits your own personal style. There is an element of this that might change the perception of the Pixel 11 camera consistency versus its predecessors. What I mean is that while it does still excel at point-and-shoot, the fact that Looks are baked into the JPEG could be a problem. There are times when I’ve thought that an image might have been better using default settings.

That said, I have stuck to “Shadows” with Contrast set to -5, Highlights to -5, Shadows to -5.5, warmth to 0.5, and Grain to “Strong.” That is a recipe I’ll probably stick with for a long time to come. It’s still weird that we can do all this at the camera level with a Pixel. Whether “normies” even use the options or just stick to the out-of-the-box default settings is another discussion for another day.

Late buy for a better Pixel

At $699, the Pixel 11 becomes a decent buy for a lot of people. For others, the distinct lack of power is something that can’t ever be overcome. I would buy this for a relative because it’ll do everything they could ever want and more. For a friend who cares about having the cutting edge in their pocket? Probably not.

A lot of the problems over the past few years on Pixel phones have come from the price tag.

Even with the discounts in and around Black Friday, the fact that you can get a device like the Galaxy S25 Ultra that’ll have better specs and lots of valuable features for around the same price. The last few generations of the Pixel have been harder to recommend because of the drawbacks versus the cost and the competition.

I said a few months ago that there is a good phone under the price hikes, and that remains unchanged. However, there are better products from the year prior that won’t compromise and are even cheaper. In a silo, you’re getting a 7/10 product at a 3/10 price. Just how that changes depends on forthcoming updates. One saving grace is that no Pixel is ever quite the same months after it rolls off the production line. A few Pixel Drops, even more discounts, and maybe a true seal of approval might be easier.

To put it into context, this was never a $900 phone and arguably never should have been. That’s somewhat a failing on Google’s part in more ways than one. At least it’s down to a palatable price that should be the Pixel baseline.

fullText:
Support for storing your driver’s license in Apple Wallet has gradually been expanding across the United States. Today, we have a status update on when the feature will go live in Connecticut, which Apple has touted as a planned partner since September 2021.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more. 

Apple Wallet ID support in 

Last week, Connecticut released its own mobile ID app for iPhone on the App Store, but without Apple Wallet support. As spotted by MacRumors, however, the app’s developer says that Apple Wallet support is “coming soon.”

While the state and developer haven’t shared any more specific information recently, a press release in May from Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont said the goal is to expand digital wallet ID support to Apple Wallet, Google Wallet, and Samsung Wallet by August 2027.

Connecticut residents have been waiting a long time for the state to launch Apple Wallet ID support. This is the first notable update we’ve had in a while.

When Apple announced support for storing your driver’s license in Apple Wallet in 2021, the company touted the following partners:

Arizona (live now)

Georgia (live now)

Connecticut

Iowa (live now)

Kentucky

Maryland (live now)

Oklahoma (live now)

Utah

So three of Apple’s launch partners have yet to roll out support for Apple Wallet IDs. Kentucky previously announced that it planned to launch support sometime in the summer, but it has missed that deadline. Evidence found within Apple’s backend code suggests that Utah support should go live soon.

You can use Apple Wallet IDs at TSA checkpoints, as well as at select businesses and organizations in person, in app, and online. It does not replace your physical license. Here are the full details on acceptance.

Apple Wallet support for IDs expanding to additional states isn’t quite as notable as it used to be. Last year, Apple launched a new Digital ID feature that is powered by your US passport. While it’s not your driver’s license, it’s a way to use your iPhone at TSA checkpoints at more than 250 airports in the United States.

title: OnePlus starts shutting down its website to ‘focus on customer support’
snippet: After shutting down its US operations earlier this year, OnePlus has quietly closed its website in some regions as it shifts to “focus on customer support.” more…
fullText:
After shutting down its US operations earlier this year, OnePlus has quietly closed its website in some regions as it shifts to “focus on customer support.”

OnePlus announced in July that it would end new product launches in the US and Europe. Just weeks later, the OnePlus 15 and other products the brand was selling in the US were sold out for good and, more recently, OnePlus rolled out its Android 17 update to transition devices to Oppo’s ColorOS instead of OxygenOS.

Now, OnePlus has fully pulled the plug on its US website, as well as some other regions.

oneplus.com/us has purged all product listings, including for accessories, with a new message saying that the brand is “streamlining” the site:

	

Following our July 16, 2026 announcement, OnePlus is streamlining this website to focus on customer support for existing OnePlus devices. For warranty, repair, and other support, please visit our support site Click.

The same applies to the OnePlus website in the Canada, and other regions, though the UK and EU countries such as France still have an operational site that mostly push Oppo products over remaining OnePlus devices, a practice that started a few months ago prior to the shutdown. The OnePlus 15, for example, is no longer available to purchase in the UK at all. Presumably, though, the OnePlus website will shut down in these regions eventually as well. 

The OnePlus website in India is unaffected and still selling devices.

The warranty website OnePlus links to appears to be more than a bit out of date, with a focus on 2023’s OnePlus Open. The most recent device mentioned is the OnePlus 13, though the page has been updated based on what we’re able to see on the Wayback Machine.

RIP OnePlus.

fullText:
This Amazon Ember TV Black Friday deal takes up to 40% off the company’s own TV brand, making it ideal for a secondary set.

Amazon Fire TVs (now known as Amazon Ember TVs) are typically quite affordable and, of course, Black Friday week is making those prices even better than usual. Case in point, the company’s most affordable TV is usually $329, but that same model is down to an incredible $199, making it ridiculously easy to recommend no matter how picky you might be about your TVs. And yes, this is the 2026 model, so you’re not buying something ancient.

Amazon Ember TV 43-inch: $199.99 ($130 off)

Amazon Ember TV 50-inch: $239.99 ($160 off)

Amazon Ember TV 55-inch: $279.99 ($180 off)

I have no idea why Amazon is so obsessed with fire-related names (Kindle, Fire TV, Ember, etc.), but it’s hard to ignore the company’s leanings toward value-heavy products that cost very little to acquire. The Amazon Ember TV lineup sports 4K resolution, support for HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG, Dolby Audio, an ambient artwork screensaver, and lots of free streaming content built-in. It’s even got Amazon Luna built in, which gives you games like Star Wars Galactic Racer for free.

fullText:
Apple’s Mac lineup is stronger than ever this year, largely thanks to the new MacBook Neo. If you’re deciding between the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

MacBook Neo 256GB: $599 (Reg. $699) 

MacBook Neo 512GB with Touch ID: $699 (Reg. $799)

13-inch M5 MacBook Air: Up to $400 off

15-inch M5 MacBook Air: Up to $400 off

MacBook Neo

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop ever, starting at $699 (currently on sale for $599). It features a solid aluminum design that comes in a range of fun colors, including Silver, Blush, Citrus, and Indigo

Unlike Apple’s other Macs, the MacBook Neo is powered by an A-series chip rather than an M-series chip. It uses the A18 Pro chip originally introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, featuring a 6-core CPU and 5-core GPU.

The MacBook Neo comes with 8GB of unified memory, with no additional RAM configuration options available. It starts with 256GB of storage, with a 512GB configuration available for an additional $100. That $100 upgrade also gets you Touch ID, which is not included in the base model.

There are some other trade-offs compared to the MacBook Air. The MacBook Neo lacks a backlit keyboard, MagSafe charging, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also has more limited USB-C connectivity and supports just one external display.

Still, the MacBook Neo offers an impressive feature set. It has a 13-inch display, up to 16 hours of battery life, a 1080p FaceTime camera, and the full macOS experience.

MacBook Neo 256GB: $599 (Reg. $699) 

MacBook Neo 512GB with Touch ID: $699 (Reg. $799)

MacBook Air

The MacBook Air, meanwhile, was updated earlier this year with Apple’s M5 chip. It starts at $1,299, making it $600 more expensive than the entry-level MacBook Air. The MacBook Air is currently on sale with a starting price of $999. 

For that $600 upgrade, the MacBook Air offers several key advantages over the MacBook Air. The M5 chip has a 10-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU, enabling better sustained performance than the MacBook Neo.

The MacBook Air also starts with 16GB of unified memory and 512GB of storage, both double the entry-level MacBook Neo. You can configure it with up to 32GB of memory and 4TB of storage, while the MacBook Neo is limited to 8GB of memory and 512GB of storage.

Apple rates the MacBook Air for up to 18 hours of video streaming and 15 hours of wireless web browsing, compared to 16 hours and 11 hours, respectively, for the MacBook Neo.

MacBook Neo vs MacBook Pro: Which should you buy?

As I wrote in my review earlier this year, I think the MacBook Neo is a great Mac, full stop … not just because of the great price. It can handle the vast majority of things most people will throw at it. This includes web browsing, basic photo and video editing, research, and much more.

The M5 MacBook Air, meanwhile, offers more power and more configuration options. This makes it a great option for people who need more storage, RAM, and power than the MacBook Neo can offer.

One of my favorite things about the MacBook Air is that it’s available in two screen sizes. The 15-inch MacBook Air is one of my favorite Apple laptops with a combination of the ultra-thin and light design and the larger screen. I think a lot of people forget it exists, but it’s an excellent choice.

To recap, I think the MacBook Neo is a great choice for everyday tasks like web browsing, email, writing, and streaming. The MacBook Air is a better fit for more demanding workflows, including photo and video editing, coding, working with large spreadsheets, and heavy multitasking.

Beyond performance, the MacBook Air offers a handful of niceties that you won’t find on the MacBook Neo. These include a backlit keyboard, a larger display with True Tone, MagSafe charging, a better webcam and speakers, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also includes Touch ID on every configuration, longer battery life, and support for two external displays.

If it’s in the budget, I think the MacBook Air is an excellent choice for all Mac shoppers. It’s plenty powerful, thin and light, and is highly configurable compared to the MacBook Neo.

Apple Watch SE 3

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a big update last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

The Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

Apple Watch Series 12

The Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a big update over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”

With the new system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

As I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.
